articles.title: Superhuman opens new Seattle office, joining wave of AI companies expanding in the region
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Superhuman , the San Francisco company formerly known as Grammarly, opened a 13,501-square-foot office in Seattle’s South Lake Union neighborhood on Tuesday, moving out of a coworking space and giving itself room to hire.
The office, at 1000 Dexter Ave. N., is opening with 50 workstations and can hold up to 80, a Superhuman representative told GeekWire via email.

Superhuman plans to keep hiring in Seattle for data engineering, data governance and data science roles. Its careers page lists 12 open positions that can be based in Seattle, including software engineering, site reliability and product management jobs.
The company joins a growing list of out-of-town AI companies expanding in the region in search of technical talent, including OpenAI in Bellevue and Anthropic in Seattle.

Grammarly acquired the Superhuman email app in July 2025 and renamed the whole company after it that October. Its CEO is Shishir Mehrotra , a former Microsoft and YouTube executive who co-founded the collaborative documents startup Coda.

The company’s suite of AI tools for work includes the Superhuman Go assistant, Mail, Docs and the Grammarly writing assistant. It has been expanding the lineup in part through acquisitions, announcing deals this year for AI detection startup GPTZero and meeting notetaker Fathom .

According to the company, the Seattle office is set up for hybrid work under a program called “ Ways of Working ,” which replaced a return-to-office mandate in January. U.S. employees choose two to five days a week in the office and get a quarterly wellness stipend ranging from $500 to as much as $2,000 depending on how often they come in, Entrepreneur reported .
We’ve asked the company for more information, including how many people it employs in Seattle and who leads the office.

articles.title: Beyond co-working: Former tech leader launches new hub for Seattle’s women founders
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: A new hub for women entrepreneurs is taking shape in Seattle and will host its official launch party tonight. Less than 10 weeks after opening, The SWELL has 53 members and quickly evolving programming that includes an accelerator, its own consulting startup and weekly “hot seats” where founders hash out challenges.

“What we’ve created is a community that happens to have a co-working space,” said founder Sally Revell . “I am not in the business of co-working. I’m in the business of building a women’s founder community, and we have a space that we convene in.”

Revell decided to launch The SWELL after 25 years in marketing leadership roles for tech companies including Google, Amazon Web Services, Philips and Intuit. Her parents’ deaths in 2024 were a “catalyst for change,” she said, prompting her to strike out as an independent consultant. But she still craved an in-person professional community.
The SWELL, an acronym for “Seattle women entrepreneurs leading and lifting,” is based at SURF Incubator, a longtime co-working and events venue in downtown Seattle.
Revell said the organization is built on three pillars:
A membership costs $200 a month and includes access to the co-working space Monday through Friday. The hub is currently capped at 75 members, and Revell is exploring a virtual program.

A survey of participants found that 40% resigned from corporate roles to launch their own ventures and 30% were laid off. An overwhelming majority have worked for big companies, and the cohort has a median of 17 years of work experience.
About 60% said they never want to return to corporate roles, and all are using AI in their business.
“There’s this movement of middle-aged women [feeling] like, ‘I’m empowered. I can choose to do something different,'” Revell said. “And when they get together, then the magic starts to happen.”

The SWELL is part of a broader push toward women-led companies. Women launched 44% of new businesses last year, according to Gusto , a payroll and HR platform. A key reason mid-career women are leaving corporate roles for entrepreneurship is that the jobs “did not line up with their needs, values, or realities,” as they struggled to balance work and caregiving, said researchers from the Rutgers Center for Women in Business .

Seattle has long been the birthplace of ventures supporting women founders and leaders. The Riveter , a pioneering, investor-backed co-working space for women, launched in 2017 but shuttered its physical locations in 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic. It pivoted to an online community with expert webinars, mentoring and retreats.

Other related efforts include Female Founders Alliance , which has grown into a national organization operated by its own investment fund, Graham & Walker; TheWMarketplace , an e-commerce platform promoting women’s businesses; and Intentionalist , a site highlighting small businesses with diverse owners.

Revell is working with other women-focused efforts in the city, including the University of Washington’s Women’s Entrepreneurial Leadership program. The SWELL recently announced a partnership with Formidable Media, a Seattle-based media and membership organization that helps women nationwide promote their businesses. And Nicole Doyle, who leads the Founder Institute’s Pacific Northwest cohort, created a custom accelerator for SWELL members that kicks off in January.

articles.title: AI founders for hire: Startup hub Foundations launches service to connect businesses with builders
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Foundations, the startup community with hubs in Seattle and San Francisco , launched a service Tuesday that lets businesses contract with its members — many of them technical founders building companies of their own — to plan, develop and implement AI systems and applications.

The service, called Foundations Design and Engineering, is designed in part to give those founders a new way to pay their bills as early-stage investment gets harder to raise . It also reflects how AI is changing tech, making software easier to build and leading some startups to act more like services firms, customizing their work for individual customers.
“I think the world of traditional consulting and startups is just absolutely going to merge,” said Aviel Ginzburg, the Seattle venture capitalist who co-founded Foundations in 2024 .

Except, in the case of Foundations Design and Engineering, the consulting won’t have the trappings of the traditional kind, he said. There is no staff of consultants and no billing by the hour . Work is priced by the project.
The pitch on the website: “Not consultants studying AI. Builders using it every day.”

The idea, he said, is to create something that “acts more like a router.” A request from a business might go to a member company already building a product in that area, a founder who knows the customer’s industry, or an early-stage founder looking for paid work.
Ginzburg said the work could have another benefit, giving founders a close look at the problems businesses are trying to solve, which can help them decide what to build.

The initials, FDE, are a play on “forward deployed engineer,” the term for engineers who embed with a customer to get technology working inside its business. Palantir popularized the role, and companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Amazon have adopted it.

Some of the details have yet to be determined. For example, Foundations is still working out how much of each contract it will keep. Ginzburg said it will vary case by case, from nothing to a double-digit percentage. Also unsettled is whether a business will sign its contract with Foundations or directly with the founder doing the work.

Prices aren’t set. In terms of a starting point, Ginzburg said founders in the community have charged $1,000 to $2,000 to spend a couple of hours with a company’s team and as much as $5,000 for an audit of how a business could use AI, with larger projects varying widely.

Foundations Design and Engineering has its roots in a group of 10 founders who were already doing consulting work and helped put the offering together. Foundations opened the service to the rest of its members Tuesday morning. A veteran Seattle startup founder will run FTE part time at first. (Ginzburg said he wasn’t ready to announce who the person is.)

Foundations counts more than 300 founders in its community, including about 30 in its founder-in-residence program . It is a public benefit corporation, a legal structure for companies that aim to turn a profit while also serving a public purpose.

It doesn’t take equity in the startups that go through the residency program, and Ginzburg said the new service is meant to bring in revenue without pulling the organization away from its mission of making founders successful.
“This is a startup,” he said. “We’ll see how it goes, but it’s going to be fun.”

articles.title: Seattle startup Chiplytics lands $4.5M to catch fake and flawed chips before they hit the market
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle startup Chiplytics today announced $4.5 million in funding to support the deployment of its microelectronics verification technology and the opening of an inspection facility in Bellport, N.Y.

The company provides authentication and quality screening of semiconductor chips and other critical electronic components. It focuses on detecting counterfeits, substitutions, inconsistencies and suspect parts before they’re assembled into machinery.
Chiplytics launched in 2022 during the COVID-driven chip shortage when manufacturers struggled to find parts and also ran into quality issues. The AI boom has created new bottlenecks in electronics.
“We’re seeing a lot of lead times now over 52 weeks for basic components,” said Stephen DiBartolomeo , president and co-founder of Chiplytics.

That leaves manufacturers with two options: wait for components from an authorized distributor or turn to independent brokers and distributors that may have the parts but are not authorized by the original manufacturer to sell them.
Chiplytics has developed technology that incorporates AI, automation and robotics to screen every electronics item for quality — rather than randomly selecting a few for testing.
“We just did an order for 50,000 parts. If you were to try and do that by hand or by sampling, it would take way too long,” DiBartolomeo said.

The company got its start through a U.S. Department of Energy program that connects entrepreneurs with technology developed in national labs to facilitate commercialization. The team worked alongside experts from Sandia National Laboratories to develop its verification platform and validated the solution with the U.S. Army, Navy and Air Force before deploying it commercially.

The startup’s newly opened inspection lab sits within a 600,000-square-foot center operated by Quality King, a major U.S. distribution company. Chiplytics supports the company’s QK Special Services, which focuses on electronics.

DiBartolomeo and Chiplytics CEO and co-founder Steven Dourmashkin knew each other from high school on Long Island, N.Y. DiBartolomeo attended the U.S. Naval Academy and worked as a cryptologic warfare officer with the National Security Agency. Dourmashkin earned degrees in mechanical engineering and launched and sold a music tech company.

The two reconnected to start a business in hardware and national security. They brought on Chief Technology Officer Connor Dempsey , an expert in semiconductor physics whom Dourmashkin knew from Cornell University.
The startup has six full-time employees plus contractors. Its R&D operations are in Seattle.

The $4.5 million in funding includes $2.5 million in seed financing and a $2 million Air Force Tactical Funding Increase award. The round was led by Scout Ventures and Waypoint Ventures. Additional investors include QKSS, Industrious Ventures, Interwoven Ventures, Seattle Alliance of Angels, and Cornell University’s Red Bear Angels.

articles.title: Duplicative services and commuter route truncation, again
articles.author: Sherwin Lee
paras: We’re about a month into the Fall shakeup, where a substantial number of service changes were implemented to improve connections to Link. This is a recurring playbook that Metro has used ever since light rail service began: identify duplicative services and restructure existing bus routes to connect to Link stations rather than running all the way into downtown Seattle.

When Northgate Link opened, Sound Transit truncated many of its 510 series routes to connect at Link instead. After Lynnwood Link, all of Community Transit’s direct services to downtown Seattle were restructured . And with the August changes , both Metro and Sound Transit no longer offer any one-seat rides from Bellevue or Issaquah to Seattle, save for the 2 Line.

Critics of this approach generally lament the loss of the one-seat ride, that trip times generally increase when factoring in wait times, and that Link is not necessarily faster point-to-point than express routes. The Sound Transit subreddit and other various community forums feature countless examples of riders testifying to that end. There is even now a “Restore 554” petition circulating among Issaquah residents, urging the restoration of a direct Issaquah-Seattle route.

The planning justifications for this type of restructuring are quite straightforward: Link provides a frequent high-capacity serve to major regional centers; instead of running costly peak-directional bus service, reinvest the hours into boosting local connecting service. This implementation aligns with Jarrett Walker’s “frequency is freedom” mantra and is generally a position this blog has supported.

In practice, however, real-world conditions can muddy the picture. Take, for example, the 554’s successor: the 556, which now provides frequent all-day service between Issaquah and Bellevue. Those previously using the 554 (or the 550 local stops along Bellevue Way) to get to Seattle must now connect at South Bellevue Station for the same trip.

These transfer conditions can greatly deteriorate due to local northbound congestion on Bellevue Way just in the short span between the I-90 off-ramp and the station bus stops. Riders agonizingly wait for traffic to crawl up Bellevue Way only to see Seattle-bound trains glide past over their heads. Even in the southbound direction, buses have to yield to northbound traffic in order to turn into the station bays, which adds travel time variability.
The physical infrastructure in between the connecting services is important too. Jarrett Walker touches on this point in one of his foundational articles on transferring:

… the unpleasantness of the connection experience depends on many details of how the connection works. If two buses or trains arrive on opposite sides of a platform, facing one another five meters apart, with their doors open at the same time, walking out of one and into the other is a pretty low level of inconvenience for most passengers. If the connection involves getting off a bus, crossing a busy street, and waiting for another bus not knowing when it will arrive, the inconvenience is much greater.

As it were, the connecting infrastructure at South Bellevue and Mercer Island stations is less than ideal. Both settings require a moderate walk (across a signalized intersection in the latter case, largely thanks to Mercer Island’s opposition to an 80th Ave transfer point) and ascending or descending to the train platform. This can add a lot of variability, particularly for those with limited mobility, on top of the wait for the connecting service.

Negative feedback is often amplified over positive feedback, as human beings are far more likely to complain about things that hurt them rather than praise the things that help them. But in many ways, what is often seen as a degradation in one part of the network typically means an improvement in another part.

554 riders, for example, might glowingly reminisce about the quick travel times across I-90, but forget about the frequent outbound reliability issues inflicted by 2nd Avenue congestion (as I so often personally experienced). And although not quite a zero sum game, the changes have meant a substantially better commute for Issaquah-Bellevue riders, among other parts of the system.

Big restructures in the regional network will invariably result in system-wide tradeoffs, but that doesn’t mean agencies’ hands are tied. Barring a miraculous way of sending buses congestion-free right up (or down) to the Link platforms, transfer penalties can be offset by improving frequency and reliability across all segments.

Making the 556 a frequent all-day route that connects to frequent 2 Line service is certainly an excellent start, but continued work on reliability improvements are always in order. This might mean more attentive maintenance to ensure fewer breakdowns of Link trains. Or it could mean stronger partnerships with WSDOT and local jurisdictions to give signal or lane priority to buses.

Whatever the solution, transit agencies cannot go it alone here. Route 8’s dramatic reliability leaps were only possible by some repainting (and other minor infrastructural improvements) from SDOT. In the same way, local jurisdictions owe it to the taxpaying public to squeeze out the full return on our massive regional investment in transit. Helping create reliable well-connected services is a small, but important step to get there.

articles.title: Zahilay Proposes Advancing RapidRide R Funding to Spur Bus Upgrades
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: King County Executive Girmay Zahilay has proposed to advance a significant portion of the funding for Seattle's RapidRide R Line , in the hopes of achieving an "accelerated delivery timeline." The project will run between Downtown Seattle and Rainier Beach and replace the current Route 7. It is currently slated for a 2032 ribbon-cutting, which Zahilay has touted the possibility of moving up.
However, early designs for the R Line are seeing pushback, over changes that are seen as degrading an existing bus route that is already one of King County Metro's busiest.

Out of the R Line's total $91.2 million expected cost, $64.4 million would be advanced into the current 2026-2027 budget, if the County Council signs off on Zahilay's "omnibus" budget proposal as transmitted last month. That cash advance comes in the wake of a decision to not seek federal dollars for the R Line, something that reflects a bleak federal transit environment and also a hope that Metro would be nimbler without federal strings attached.

Metro is planning R Line upgrades in conjunction with major planned repaving work on Rainier Avenue being advanced by the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). An overhaul of the corridor from S Jackson Street to S Walden Street in Mount Baker, being paired with maintenance work on S Henderson Street in Rainier Beach, is expected to cost the city more than $100 million and provides an opportunity to include changes like new bus lanes, enhanced sidewalks, or separated bike facilities.

"Our goal in accelerating this funding is to build a strong partnership with SDOT and bolster our shared commitment to this project," Callie Craighead, Zahilay's press secretary, told The Urbanist . "King County Metro and the Seattle Department of Transportation are actively working to develop plans for shared investments along the RapidRide R alignment that minimize construction and roadway impacts, save costs, and support an accelerated delivery timeline. We heard from SDOT that they would like King County to make a stronger funding commitment to the project to avoid another situation where uncertain funding leads to delays or pauses in the project."
As a bus route that bisects Zahilay's former county council district, the new County Executive has turned the corridor upgrade into one of his administration's major transit priorities.

"I'm challenging Metro to do anything in our power to work with the City of Seattle to build a quality product as fast as possible," Zahilay said at a Metro open house for the project in August. "Every single weekday people are relying on this [route], so I wouldn't be advocating for a RapidRide R on a personal level if I didn't know that it was going to make the service better."

The Route 7 currently carries more than 11,000 daily riders on weekdays, making it the busiest route in Metro's network that never leaves the City of Seattle. With light rail running along MLK Way in parallel with the Route 7 for much of its route, the bus is often the choice for shorter local trips, or downtown trips for riders who aren't able to easily get to the faster train.

Officials hope the R Line will be significantly faster than Route 7, in part due to bus stop consolidation. But when early design concepts presented at open houses this summer showed that a significant number of existing bus stops were on the table to be eliminated with the conversion to the R Line, concerns mounted that current 7 riders would have longer walks to access transit than they do today, and people with disabilities might lose access altogether.

The maps that Metro recently presented resurfaced some of the same issues that plagued the project in its first iteration, before being officially put back on the shelf in 2021 due to financial constraints.

"A RapidRide would reduce the number of stops on the route, which would make it harder for people who currently rely on their local route," Urbanist contributor Ashley Archibald wrote that year , in a story that references many of the same issues that community members are bringing up now.

In the name of speeding up trips, Metro's initial concept would have consolidated 67 stops along the entire corridor into 45, counting both northbound and southbound trips. Along the northern segment of Rainier Avenue, for example, three northbound stops between Judkins Park Station and 12th Avenue would be converted into just one stop at S Dearborn Street. Heading south from Judkins Park, riders would have only one opportunity – at S Walker Street – to deboard before getting to Mount Baker Station.

Estimates produced by Metro in 2020 showed a travel time savings of 7.3 minutes to 11.7 minutes with the R Line during peak hours by 2040, but a big portion of those savings were expected to come from bus lanes that SDOT has actually implemented along some segments of Rainier Avenue since that time. Metro has not yet released any updated time savings data for its current concepts that reflect the gains that have already been made in reliability for the 7.

"There's a lot of folks using the bus to travel locally within Rainier Valley, and commuting to downtown as efficiently as possible is not necessarily the top priority for a lot of folks who are using transit right now on this road," Anna Zivarts, founder and executive director of the Nondrivers Alliance, told The Urbanist .

This past weekend, Zivarts hosted a Route 7 ride with local mobility advocates and elected officials to present them with an up-close view of who is actually using the bus today. In attendance were State Senator Rebecca Saldaña and Port Commissioner Toshiko Hasegawa – both are campaigning to become the next King County Councilmember for District 2 – as well as Seattle Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck and 37th Legislative District state house candidate Kelabe Tewolde. The event was timed with the annual Week Without Driving .

Rinck noted that Rainier Avenue was included in her "Better Bus Lanes" budget proposal that was unanimously approved last year, along with the successful Denny Way bus lanes that were installed this summer .

"We've made progress on bus lanes. We now need the frequency to match the need, and so that is why I'm really excited about RapidRide R, particularly from the frequency components that will come with it," Rinck told The Urbanist following the ridealong. "I have some outstanding concerns about the stop elimination plan, and I'm curious to learn more about what the county is thinking on that front. But the city is going to need to be a partner in those infrastructure improvements to support that project coming online. I'm really committed to working with riders and future riders of the 7/RapidRide R to make sure that it's meeting community needs."

Metro spokesperson Al Sanders told The Urbanist that the agency is still actively developing an updated proposal for RapidRide R, ahead of a potential King County Council vote confirming the route's alignment and planned stop locations next month.

"Rescoping work for the R Line is still underway," Sanders said. "Metro is using what we’ve been hearing from the community, along with updated technical analysis, to help identify the highest-priority elements of the project. Because the corridor and travel patterns have changed since the original concept was developed, this step is critical to making sure the final design reflects current needs."

While the proposals presented this summer weren't much changed from the previous iteration of the R Line, the refreshed plans may be more aligned with current needs along the corridor and more responsive to critiques from riders.

"While we are still compiling all of the input, we have heard strong support for increased investment in transportation infrastructure in South Seattle and that riders want fast, reliable transit service throughout the Rainier Valley. We are also hearing that stop locations and walking distance are important to Route 7 riders," Sanders continued.
Craighead said that Zahilay's office has been engaged with Metro when it comes to what that updated proposal looks like.

"Our team is actively working with King County Metro to develop a RapidRide R alignment proposal to transmit to the King County Council," Craighead told The Urbanist . "Executive Zahilay and members of his staff joined open houses about the project this summer to hear community feedback directly and are working with Metro to incorporate that feedback into the proposal. Delivering long-promised and long-overdue transit investments to South Seattle continues to be a priority for the Executive."

It will ultimately fall on Zahilay's office and the Metro team to thread the needle on what is already an intensely beloved bus, even if frequent bus bunching and overcrowding does get on riders' nerves.

"If we're trying to entice people into riding transit who have other options already, that's a different priority than meeting the needs of people who are already relying on transit and don't have other options in the Rainier Valley, and that's a very large population here," Zivarts said. "And so I worry with this RapidRide proposal, it's focused more on the theoretical person who might be enticed to ride transit if their commute was shorter, versus the people who need it to get to the grocery store, the pharmacy, or whatever they need to do along this corridor."

articles.title: If Seattle wants more corner stores, it has to figure out the Volunteer Park Cafe garden patio
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The patio in 2021 as the cafe reopened under its new owners

With a history as a flashpoint between Seattle’s view of itself as a modern, urbanist city and the realities of its neighborhood, single family-friendly zoning, the latest land use kerfuffle around Capitol Hill’s Volunteer Park Cafe has been baking for a while.

The cafe and market at 17th and Galer is open and serving but VPC’s garden patio has been shut down. According to a sign posted by the cafe , the city has prohibited customers from entering the garden.
“Please direct any questions or comments to City Attorney Erika Evans and Assistant City Attorney Cindi Williams ,” the cafe’s management helpfully advises.

They also might want to include the city inspector who filed the first report on the patio issued in 2024. That spring, the inspect was following up on a complaint over an agreement forged with the cafe years earlier during initial disputes with neighbors over the opening of a busy cafe in the middle of the residential neighborhood just down Galer from Volunteer Park :
Rear yard not to be used for on site dining, rear yard gates to have signs permanently affixed stating “Private Yard, Not for Restaurant Use” and rear yard gates to be self-closing”.

That April inspection kicked off two years of follow-ups by the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections with visits to the cafe to check on the patio issue and ongoing complaints about the alleged violations of the cafe’s neighborhood agreement and land use rules.
Things finally came to a head this summer as an irritated neighbor had had enough:

I thought the Volunteer Park Cafe had finally ceased using the back yard but that all changed this morning. This is exhausting and I’m sure not fun for you either but I feel like, if we let this go, thay will assume they can continue violating the use restrictions of their Conditional Use. My understanding was that the City fined them previously; we hadn’t seen any violations since then. We still support the concept of the neighborhood restaurant–we just want them to abide by the conditions.Please let me know if you need anything further and keep us informed.

The same SDCI inspector concurred after a July visit, writing, “They are still allowing on site dining activities in backyard. I inspected and customers were taking food and beverages from inside to backyard thru the propped open gate to backyard.”
“They have proven for many years now to just disregard the code requirements,” he concluded, advising advancing the violation notices to the “fining stage” —
unless they remove all tables in backyard, stop propping the gate open and all staff at point of ordering ask the customer, “ do you want to sit inside or on the sidewalk—the backyard is closed?”

With the City Attorney now along for the ride, the threats of fines and legal action have closed the garden patio off and, for now, ended the latest chapter in the cafe’s complicated relationship with the neighborhood.

That relationship has now spanned nearly two decades and multiple owners. CHS reported in August — as the patio fight was going on behind the scenes — on the five-year anniversary of the cafe’s restart under new owners and VPC’s place as a “gold standard for neighborhood spots” in the city.

It has been 15 years since the original ownership, neighbors, and the city made peace with an agreement to allow the cafe to operate at the corner that has been home to neighborhood businesses including cafes and markets for decades.

Under Seattle’s existing land use code, running a cafe or corner store inside a primarily residential neighborhood is legally fraught. Most existing neighborhood spots survive only as “nonconforming uses,” grandfathered relics from decades-old commercial zoning, or operate under rigid conditional use permits negotiated under the wispy clouds of neighbor complaints. Those permits come attached to specific, legally binding operating restrictions that can govern everything from hours and delivery times to outdoor seating and gate latches.

Because current code treats neighborhood-embedded commercial activity as an intrusion into low-density residential zones, operators face vulnerability. A neighbor complaint can bring city code compliance inspectors to the door and trigger escalation and fines.

With the Volunteer Park Cafe continuing to be held up as an example of how Seattle’s new comprehensive plan update is hoped to make it easier to open and operate corner stores and neighborhood businesses by re-legalizing commercial uses directly within residential blocks, Seattle is going to also need to learn how to sort out issues like the VPC garden patio. Hopefully those solutions are more innovative than shutting it down.

articles.title: Capitol Hill #4 in 2026 Seattle felony drug dealing charges
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: 2026 cases through July (Image: King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office)
King County prosecutors say they are filing 15 felony drug dealing charges a month so far in 2026 with Capitol Hill cases ranking fourth among the city’s crackdown hot spots.
The King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office says it filed 106 felony drug dealing charges through July, with Capitol Hill a key enforcement hub outside Seattle’s central downtown core.

According to the update, nine felony dealing cases originated in Capitol Hill ranking it among the city’s most active areas for prosecution behind Belltown (18), Downtown (15), and the Chinatown-International District’s 12th and Jackson intersection (13).
Capitol Hill came in just below 12th and Jackson and the city of Auburn in the overall tally.

County prosecutors said that illicit synthetic opioids and stimulants dominate the neighborhood networks. Nearly 80% of all filed cases countywide involved fentanyl, methamphetamine, or both, with fentanyl present in 66% of charges.
The caseload arrives amid an ongoing overdose crisis, with King County recording 446 confirmed fatal overdoses through July 2026, following 914 fatal overdoses in 2025.
“Drug dealers who profit from fentanyl and meth are fueling a crisis that is devastating families across King County,” Prosecuting Attorney Leesa Manion said in the announcement.
While city municipal prosecutors handle low-level possession, county prosecutors pursue felony distribution cases referred by law enforcement.

articles.title: Seattle Council holding first of two ‘all-day’ public hearings on Wilson budget proposal
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The Seattle City Council will hold its first of two public hearings on the 2027-2028 budget Tuesday afternoon. Get comfortable. It’s an epically long session:

The public hearing will begin with remote public comment at 1 p.m. Members of the public can register online to give remote public comment between 12 p.m. and 3 p.m. Everyone who signs up during that time period will be given the opportunity to speak.

The public hearing will then continue with in-person public comment at 5 p.m. In-person public commenters can sign up outside of Council Chambers starting at 4:30 p.m. The public hearing will conclude after everyone has had a chance to speak.

CHS reported here on Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposal which would wipe out an inherited $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves. The proposal would cut roughly $50 million annually in General Fund spending by eliminating 128 positions and aligning departmental budgets with historical costs, pairing these cuts with $50 million in shuffled funding — primarily leveraging JumpStart payroll tax revenues to cover core services and homelessness programs — and enabling the city, Wilson says, to project balanced budgets through 2030 without drawing on reserves.
Budget chair Dan Strauss next week will lead the process ad council members will be briefed by staff on policy considerations before officially proposing potential amendments to the mayor’s proposal.

District 3 representative Council President Joy Hollingsworth has signaled her support for continued police and anti-crime investments, joining a call for the mayor to strengthen her public safety plan . articles.title: Twenty-Three Washington State Ferry Engineers Called in Sick Monday
articles.author: Meg van Huygen
paras: On Monday morning, the Washington State Ferries (WSF) announced that 13 of its 18 ferries were out of service, after 23 engine room employees “called in sick.” Additionally, every qualified employee subsequently refused to fill in for the absent workers.

For passengers, the consequences were immediate: missed connections, disrupted commutes, delayed medical visits, and general uncertainty ensued. Island communities are especially vulnerable to ferry outages, obviously, because when a vessel loses sailings, alternative travel is usually limited, expensive, or just plain impossible to find. “The ferries cannot run without these roles being filled,” a graphic read on WSF’s Instagram account . “All of the employees calling in sick and declining to fill those vacancies are represented by the Marine Engineers’ Beneficial Association (MEBA), who represent engine room employees.” WSF’s Instagram post continued: “We understand how disruptive this is to thousands of Washingtonians. We expect our employees to return to work as soon as possible.”

* * * Just below the water’s surface, though, lurked more context. WSF has suffered from severe staffing issues since at least 2020, and it’s an open secret that the system relies heavily on worker overtime to keep the boats running. Some reports say that engine room workers typically work seven days a week, and they often exceed 1,500 hours of overtime per year. In 2024, MEBA representative Eric Winge told Q13 FOX that “decades of underinvestment and poor management decisions by state administrators” were key factors contributing to the staffing crisis. “Engine room staff are often called on to work backshifts,” Winge also said, “often sleeping in their cars and at the docks.”

Plus, each vessel requires three or four marine engineers aboard, as mandated by the US Coast Guard, and safety rules greatly limit the agency’s ability to substitute workers on short notice. The staffing shortage in the engine room is so dire that if a single worker calls out sick and can’t be replaced, it can dock a whole ferry .

Another central complication in Monday’s incident is that the engineers are legally prohibited from striking under state law . Although the work cancellation was called a “sick-out” by some, WSF has not confirmed that the absences were coordinated. MEBA Secretary-Treasurer Roland “Rex” Rexha told KOMO News the union did not authorize the incident either . “The union didn’t take any action today,” Rexha said. “This is not a coordinated effort by any means.” The distinction matters. WSF employees are legally allowed to use sick leave when they cannot report for work, per the state, but a coordinated labor stoppage would be illegal. So why did this happen?

An important moving part here is the age-old pay gap between above-deck and below-deck workers at WSF. Masters, mates, and pilots working on the bridge can earn up to 25 percent more than the similarly licensed and experienced engine room staff, while workers on the deck get about 20 percent more than same-level workers below deck. The gulf between wages is even more stark, considering the amount of overtime that WSF workers put in—the difference paid at time and a half across the board, adds up. Another possible mitigating factor is the MEBA workers’ contract , which workers are latterly unhappy with. Negotiations for their upcoming 2027–2029 contract ended in July after they went to arbitration. While the contract dispute focused partially on pay, bargaining attempts also included negotiations on WSF staffing levels and overall workload, to ease stress and burnout among engine room crew members, along with securing proposed provisions for potential future bargaining within the broader contract lifecycle. As such, in July, MEBA’s unionized workers were seeking a 20 percent wage increase for their upcoming 2027–2029 contract. This pay raise would mean their salaries would approach the salaries of their above-deck coworkers as well as the pay grade for the same jobs in private-sector or other regional maritime system equivalents.

Instead, the arbitration decision was for a zero percent raise in 2027 and a wage reopener in 2028, which allows both parties to revisit the issue then. Per their existing 2025–2027 contract, MEBA-represented workers received an annual wage increase of 4 percent on July 1, 2026, as they also had a year prior. Rexha, however, told Seattle Times on Monday that the October work cancellations aren’t related to MEBA’s contract negotiations or any collective bargaining effort. As a possible nod to this wage parity issue, WSF wrote on their October 5 Instagram post: “The employees who work in the engine room play a vital role in providing WSF’s safe service. This is why Chief Engineers have a base salary of $157,000, and can make more than $350,000 a year with overtime, as well as annual sick and vacation leave, and retirement accrual.” All of this came to a head this summer.

On June 17, 2026, the engineers’ union, MEBA, held a press conference at Seattle’s Colman Dock to express concern about WSF staffing levels, overtime demands, and the serious wage disparity among workers that could make recruiting and retaining credentialed marine engineers even more difficult in the future. Per the union’s weekly Telex Times publication, a survey of WSF engine room personnel found “widespread dissatisfaction, with more than 55% reporting low morale and over 60% saying they are likely to retire or seek employment elsewhere.”

The same issue of Telex Times pointed out that buying new ferries would not fix the problem, as many have suggested. Because engineers operate, maintain, and repair engines and other mechanical systems that allow the boats to sail safely, having a full complement of them on board is crucial before a vessel can depart. “Billions of dollars are being spent on new ferries,” Winge wrote, “but if the state doesn’t close this wage gap, we won’t have enough licensed crew to operate and repair the new hybrid electric vessels when they come into service.”

While all of this has created a powder keg in the ferry engine rooms, multiple reports allege there was another trigger. Reportedly, a chief marine engineer—the same role whose pay was coincidentally mentioned as an example in WSF’s October 5 announcement—disobeyed a captain’s direct order earlier in the summer, and the captain’s union was in a dispute with WSF over whose fault it was. The incident between the captain and the chief engineer was supposedly a final straw on the camel’s back, further exacerbating the ongoing pressure and disgruntlement that’s been building for months, and it resulted in Monday’s supposed “sick-out.” * * *

The scale of the disruption highlighted how fast a worker dispute can become a transportation crisis in a watery part of the world like ours. Most of WSF’s ferry routes were effectively kneecapped, leaving thousands of islanders, commuters, and holidaymakers alike on hold all day. The Mukilteo–Clinton route—WSF’s busiest run for vehicles—was down to one boat on Monday, rather than two boats orbiting one another per usual, creating a two-hour-minimum delay. The Vashon–Tahlequah route was in service but experiencing delays as well. All other routes experienced either route cancellations or total service suspensions, and Western Washington’s would-be ferry passengers were left only with service updates and rebooking measures. In a statement released Monday by Washington state Governor Bob Ferguson , who met with MEBA that morning, he said: “My expectation is that every vessel on every route is fully operational no later than the first vessel sailing [Tuesday] morning.” His prophecy came true, with WSF’s system mostly returning to normal service with some delays on Tuesday. The Stranger emailed several union organizers and WSF execs asking for comment on Monday’s alleged “sick-out” incident, none replied by press time.

Although the boats are back on the water as of Tuesday, WSF still must resolve its long-term worker compensation, staffing shortage, and retention challenges. Monday’s cancellations show that fleet capacity alone does not guarantee dependable service; they also need skill, experience, and willingness.

The incident has once again exposed the fragility of a ferry system—the second-largest in the world, just behind BC Ferries—that had recently emphasized improvements in service and staffing. Overall, the so-called “sick-out” incident, whether coordinated or coincidental, proved to be a real test of WSF’s endurance, resilience, and adaptability—one that it didn’t exactly pass with flying colors.

articles.title: Quickies
articles.author: Dan Savage
paras: 1. I’m a bisexual man who’s new to Seattle. I was just invited to my first sex party by some new friends. The problem: I’m training to be a teacher and my therapist thinks this could be problematic for my career. I am now considering backing out to the party and stopping all related activities. My question: How far do you think this adjustment should go? Should I embrace priestly behavior or say “fuck it” and live my life?

Teachers are held to a double standard. While teachers, like other people, are allowed to have sex lives, we expect teachers to keep all proof that they’ve ever had, might ever have, or might ever want to have sex off the internet. That’s an impossible standard for modern adults to meet, given that most relationships get their start online. Still, so long as your online presence is PG13 — so long as your new Seattle friends aren’t planning to livestream this sex party — you’ll be fine… probably?
P.S. With apologies to Inigo Montoya: You used the expression “priestly behavior.” I do think it conveys what you think it conveys.
P.P.S. This letter writer hasn’t been in Seattle long and he’s already invited to his first sex party — looks like the Seattle Freeze is dead, huh?
2. Should oral be included when adding up your body count? I say no (straight man), wife (straight woman) says yes.

So, you walk into your living room and your wife is on her knees sucking your best friend’s dick. Is your wife cheating on you? If you can honestly answer that question with a “no,” then you don’t have to include oral-only encounters in your body count.

3. The reelection of Donald Trump, the Pelicot horrors , and now the Cornell gang rape — how the fuck am I supposed to fuck men anymore? A threesome with two men is my ultimate fantasy and now it feels like I can never take the risk. If homosexuality was a choice, I’d choose it. What is a straight woman to do?

While they’re not all Trumps, Pelicots, or Cornell frat boys, for your own safety you have to assume that any man you’re interacting with — sexually or otherwise — could be a Trump, etc., until you’re as certain as you can be that he’s not a Trump, etc. (“Not all men, but always a man.”) And if you do decide to have that threesome, do it with a friend of yours, not a friend of his, and do it sober.

P.S. My heart goes out to all the survivors of rape and sexual violence out there who are having to slog through another news cycle like this — it’s awful. If you need to check out from the news or men or both right now, don’t hesitate to do it. But please check back in for the midterms, if only to ruin this adjudicated rapist’s day.
4. I’m a straight and I love pegging my boyfriend. I don’t think it makes him any less straight. My girlfriends disagree.
P.S. I hope your boyfriend enjoys it too.

5. Long-time listener! A few months back, over the course of several shows, you casually used the word “dint.” This is a very uncommon and rare word usage in the United States — and yet you’ve used it at least twice in less than a month. I learned the word in the Episcopal church choir many decades ago, but rarely any other time. Can you tell me how it became part of your vernacular this year?

I don’t know when that particular four-letter first entered my vocabulary, but it wasn’t this year. This is from a column I wrote more fifteen years ago: “A gay male football fan who says, ‘Sorry, lady, I’m gay,’ is going to be believed because no one is secretly straight —and some gay men are going to find him more attractive by dint of how straight he seems.” And I go on to use “dint” again in the very next sentence.

P.S. Em dashes are being cited everywhere as evidence that a writer is using AI. That column from fifteen years ago has eleven em dashes in it, and I have emails going back thirty years from editors begging me to use fewer em dashes! If the chatbots scraped my content, their use of em dashes might be my fault. So, to any “writers” out there who’ve gotten busted for em dashes suddenly appearing in their writing three years ago… sorry, not sorry?

6. I’m a happily married woman with four children, married over fifteen years. We have a very healthy sex life. My husband goes down on me every time before we have sex, which his great, but I want him to toss my salad. I want to experience this is at least once but I don’t know how to broach the topic. He joked about it once and I said “you could do that” and he looked shocked and said “it sounds like you actually want me to.” I obviously should’ve said “yes, I actually want you to” but I was afraid he thought it was gross. How can I get my husband to want to do this? Even better, how can I make him think it was his idea?

There are no magic words — there’s no spell that will make your husband bring up eating your ass again, there’s no potion that will make him think eating your ass was his idea — which means you’re gonna have to use your regular, non-magical words and do the regular, non-magical thing of asking for what you want. That’s how the magic happens.

P.S. So, I have a friend who’s into piss. He told his boyfriend he “stumbled over” some “freaky piss porn” on social media and his boyfriend nodded and said, yeah, guys into piss are freaks . Ten years later, my friend and his by now ex-boyfriend ran into each other at a piss party. That’s how they found out— too late — that they were both into piss. Anyway, my friend made a common mistake: he brought up his niche sexual interest but framed it negatively so that he could deny interest if his partner reacted with disgust. Which his partner did — but his partner wasn’t actually disgusted by piss, he was just mirroring my friend’s negatively.

It’s possible the same might’ve happened when your husband brought up tossing your salad — just with an incredulous/joking frame, instead of a negative one. My advice: don’t ask your husband if he was joking when he brought up tossing your salad because he might say he was even if he wasn’t. Instead, tell him you weren’t joking when you said you wanted him to do it.
P.P.S. That was a really long P.S., wasn’t it?
7. You once told readers where to send their unwanted dildos. I got two new ones and have one old one that I want to get rid of. Where should I send them in 2026?
We live in a target-rich environment where old dildos are concerned — so, the first billionaire, federal agency, or rightwing news site that came to mind is probably the right one.

8. My husband quit smoking ten years ago. He recently started again and tried to hide it from me. This has me wondering what else is he might be hiding. He started doing different things in bed. Good things, things I enjoy, but different. Do I just enjoy the change or do I assume that he’s learned these new tricks from someone else and he’s keeping an affair from me too?

If the possibility that your husband is cheating doesn’t bother you — if you’re possibly toly — and if you’re enjoying the new tricks (who wouldn’t?) and can tolerate the smoking (I couldn’t), you don’t have to choose between enjoying the change and continuing to turn a blind eye to the affair your husband may (or may not!) be having.
My Folsom wasn’t because I didn’t — maybe next year!

10. My husband has always wanted to watch me have sex with another man and I’ve come around on the idea but I’m worried about catching feeling for someone, which I do pretty easily when I’m fucking someone. Game it out for me?

Even if you can’t control for catching feelings — even if you’ve caught feelings for every man you’ve ever fucked — you can control for being able to do anything about those feelings. So, while you’ll obviously want the other guy to be someone you feel safe with and find attractive… and while you’ll need him to be a guy who’s into the idea of fucking a woman in front of her husband… you don’t have to go with someone local and available. Get on Feeld and find a bull who’s happily married himself and/or lives far the fuck away. Then even if you were to catch feelings during your first fuck, he’s not going to leave his wife to be with you (probably) and/or move to the city where you live (most likely) to be closer to you.
11. Forgive me if you’ve already thought of this, but would the opposite of a DADT arrangement — “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell” — be a DTDT arrangement? DTDT: “Do Tell! Do Tell!”

12. I’m attracted to a friend of my husband. Like, dripping wet attracted. Feral and chemical. Never going to act on it, have a great sex life with my husband, we are monogamous. Nothing is ever going to happen. I can keep this to myself, right?

Keep it to yourself unless your husband is DTDT. But you’re free to get wet around this guy, excuse yourself from a dinner party to masturbate about this guy, and to think about this guy while you’re fucking your husband.

13. I’m a lesbian and my girlfriend of a six months is married to a man. They had kids before my girlfriend realized she was gay. They made a “joint decision” three months ago to stay married and live under one roof until their kids are out of high school. (I put “joint” in quotes because I was not consulted.) They still share a bed, although they do not have sex, and their youngest won’t be out of high school until 2035. I find this unacceptable. My girlfriend’s relationship with her ex is amicable while ours is increasingly characterized by conflict due to a “joint decision” I was excluded from. This is crazy, right?
Got problems? Yes, you do! Email your question for the column to mailbox@savage.love!

articles.title: Slog AM: Oil Prices Show No Signs of Dropping, the Disney Adult Editor of Washington’s Second-Biggest Newspaper is in Hot Water, Sailors Mutiny Suppressed in the Tsar’s Salish Sea Fleet
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: The allegations against the Spokesman Review’s suspended editor in chief are extensive: When longtime Spokesman Review editor Rob Curley was suspended by the paper’s owner in August, followed by a vote of no confidence from his staff, a lot of people wondered what the hell was going on. As the city was engulfed in flames at the time, there were bigger priorities to attend to, but the details are out now, courtesy of a lengthy investigation by RANGE Media and Investigate West . The details are worth reading in full for yourself, but in short, newsroom employees accuse their Disney adult editor of compromising the editorial independence of the paper, nepotistic hiring, lying about reporters being paid with community donations, retaliation, cronyism, and, worst of all hiring a personally loyal but “disorganized and unproductive editor who often shopped online for magician supplies while in the office.” Curley has long survived criticism with the backing of one of Spokane’s richest families, which owns the paper, but his suspension, his staff’s vote of no confidence, and the public allegations he now faces make him seem destined to be sealed back into the Disney Vault for good.

We’re Gone! A Dinosaur’s Story: Wandering around Minoru Yamsaki’s delightful United States Science Pavilion this weekend, I noticed something: the triceratops and the stegosaurus statues are gone. Luckily for me Seattle Times reporter Ann Duan noticed their absence, too, and actually looked into it . Some of the animatronics from the recently closed dinosaur exhibit, including the tyrannosaur that haunted my dreams as a child, are still on display near the main entrance. However, there is still an important animatronic missing, one that also used to occupy the space near the interior stairs, and which no one seems to remember, even though it talked, and sometimes, killed.

Production of the pro-ICE action film in Montana isn’t going great: Speaking of racist movies shot in the Pacific Northwest, production is back on for the Daily Wire-produced movie about ICE fighting antifa and MS-13 in Minneapolis after the local film board shut down filming in Livingston, Montana over resident complaints.

The state legislative districts redrawn to empower one of Washington’s few Latino majority communities might be in trouble: Washington state Republicans have dragged the matter through the courts for years after redistricting, worried that empowering the Latino majority will result in farmworkers electing Democrats over the Republicans who serve agribusiness. The US Supreme Court just kicked the decision back down to the lower courts to decide, the Seattle Times reports .

The farmworker movement is making a play in the 14th district, which you can familiarize yourself with in this new Yakima Herald profile . Here’s what Democratic challenger Chelsea Dimas has to say about the lack of collective bargaining rights for farmworkers, the movement’s top issue in the legislature last session that was torpedoed by Democrats crossing the aisle: “This last session I went up with [United Farm Workers] and many of the workers to try to lobby for this law… unfortunately, that didn’t pass. It is something I’m incredibly passionate about, and that is something I am willing to challenge my own party on because I truly believe that farmworkers should no longer continue to be the exception in our unionization and collective bargaining laws.”

“Minimal early morning cancellations” is how the Washington State Ferries rosily described operations this morning after yesterday’s wildcat strike of engineers over low pay and understaffing. That’s not “no cancellations” … Ferry workers pulling a sickout is only the proximate cause of the ferry service disruption. The ultimate cause is the political decision made by Gov. Bob Ferguson to not raise the necessary taxes to fund government services because it is unpopular, and therefore refusing wage increases for state workers despite the skyrocketing cost of living, which means an effective pay cut to real wages. If you push people to their limit, they will push back. And even if there are only a few dozen of them, unlike larger public employee unions, their scarcity makes them irreplaceable. As all union workers know, there are Straits of Hormuz everywhere for those with the eyes to see them.

Oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz have reached pre-war levels, so why is gas still so expensive? One big reason is transportation costs. Hazard pay and warzone insurance isn’t cheap, raising costs for suppliers that have to be recouped down the line from you, the consumer. Bloomberg’s description of supertankers running dark close to the Omani shore at night is harrowing. The Saudis tried to avoid the Hormuz hazard by using their pipeline to the Red Sea export terminals instead, but it was bombed.

Canadian crude is also expensive for this reason —it costs a lot to liquify tar sands and ship it from the heart of North America to coastal export terminals and refineries, which is why the Canadian and US governments built the Dakota Access Pipeline through Native American communities. They failed to build the Keystone XL pipeline after a federal lawsuit in Montana, so to reduce transportation costs and make the oil sands more lucrative, the Canadians want a new pipeline west across the Rockies terminating at the BC coast right above Washington’s border. KOUW reports Gov. Ferguson is worried increased tanker traffic would endanger orcas, and you’ve got to expect he’s real tired of talking about ships right now.

Houthis encircle Saudi-backed forces in a key city: Saudi-backed forces advanced across some of the flat coastal plain around the Bab al-Mandab Strait yesterday, which is where all the oil shipping is, and thus captured a lot of international headlines, even though they have since lost those gains. But the Houthis captured something more important, a number of highland villages south of Taiz, cutting the only road to one of Yemen’s largest cities, the Associated Press reports . Saudi-backed forces have long held Taiz even as the Houthis reached the outskirts, but Ansar Allah has in the past few days advanced across the ridgelines in the countryside outside the city and encircled it. The fight is now a grim siege. Without Taiz, the Saudi-backed faction has little claim to power.

I tried to see The History of Concrete this weekend but it was sold out, so instead I watched two hours of behind-the-scenes interviews on the creation of Everybody Loves Raymond . I think the cast and crew give John Wilson a real run for his money, so instead of my usual appeal to watch some foreign documentary shot on Mini DV tape in 2002, I instead offer you the late Doris Roberts knowing her character Marie Barone better than most of you know yourselves.

If you don’t, call King County Elections to see what’s up. Not registered? It’s not too late! You can register online through October 26, and even register and vote in-person through Election Day. articles.title: A medieval manuscript has confounded scholars for centuries. Have they been reading it wrong all this time?
articles.author: Philip Oltermann European culture editor
paras: Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable text

It has been called the world’s most mysterious manuscript: a medieval set of pages filled with botanical drawings, astronomical diagrams, pictures of nude women and indecipherable text. Claimed at various times to be a book in a lost language, a musical score, an instruction manual or just an elaborate hoax, the so-called Voynich manuscript’s true meaning has defied cryptographers and codebreakers for centuries.

Now, new research offers an explanation for why a scholarly consensus over this enduring puzzle has been so hard to come by: not only because its truth is so profoundly mysterious – but because everyone has been reading its pages in the wrong order.

articles.title: Columbus’ own writings reveal how tightly religion and conquest were intertwined from the start
articles.author:
<name>Peter C. Mancall, Distinguished Professor and Professor of the Humanities, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/peter-c-mancall-313858"/>
paras: Few historic figures are as divisive as Christopher Columbus. For some, in both Spain and the United States , he remains a great hero , an explorer who found a “new world.” He is reviled by others who see him as an arrogant conqueror: the first European to enslave Indigenous Americans , and the man who launched ecological destruction in the Western Hemisphere .

As a historian who writes about early encounters between Europeans, Indigenous Americans and Africans in North America, I believe it is important to recapture this period as much as we can from existing documents – including Columbus’ own writings. Those texts reveal the enormous importance the push to spread Christianity played in Europeans’ colonial plans from the start.

In my 2026 book , “Contested Continent: The Struggle for North America, c. 1000-1680,” I describe how Europeans’ religious desires shaped the creation of American colonies that benefited conquerors, at a high cost to those they displaced or enslaved. In the Americas, the linkage of religious purpose and the eager pursuit of glory and wealth began in 1492.

Long before Columbus set sail, Europeans were already eager to expand their faith – and territory. Centuries earlier, Crusaders had ridden into the Middle East to reclaim what they saw as their holy land from Muslims.

That contest took place in Spain as well. Muslim armies had invaded from North Africa in the 700s, and Muslim rulers eventually governed much of the peninsula. Spanish and Portuguese leaders waged the Reconquista , a centuries-long war that concluded with the 1492 expulsion of Jews and the defeat of the last Muslim stronghold in Granada.
By then, the Portuguese had laid claim to uninhabited mid-Atlantic islands, including the Azores and Madeira .

They also colonized the Canary Islands and forced local inhabitants into slavery on their plantations. In 1479, Portugal ceded control of the the Canary Islands to Spain in a treaty to end a war between the two nations. Spaniards expanded the importation of enslaved Africans to produce sugar.

Columbus wanted to find the fastest way to get to the southwest Pacific to bring home exotic spices . He searched for sponsors to support his idea that Europeans could reach the the Spice Islands by sailing west across the Atlantic. Spain’s Queen Isabella of Castile and King Ferdinand II of Aragon provided funds to fit out three ships.

After his return, Columbus wrote a letter to his patrons , describing how, after 33 days at sea, he landed in the Bahamas . He labeled the people he met “Indios” because he thought he had reached Asia. The name stuck even though he was wrong about his point of arrival.

On his first voyage, Columbus claimed and renamed multiple islands, starting with San Salvador, or “Holy Savior.” “To the first of them I have given the name of our blessed Saviour, (with) whose aid I have reached this and all the rest,” he wrote . He named places after his patrons, too, along with other Christian names, such as Santa Maria de Concepion – Holy Mary of the Conception – and Navidad, Nativity.

He also laid claim to at least some Tainos. “I took by force some Indians from the first island,” he wrote , reporting that he wanted to teach them Spanish so they could “tell us what they knew” about environments new to him.

Soon after he returned to Spain, Columbus had the text printed . He wrote that “the whole of Christendom should rejoice” at discoveries he had made for his patrons “for all the glory they will receive when so many peoples turn to our Holy Faith.”
Within a few short years his words spread across Europe, translated from one language into another. Ferdinand and Isabella named him “ Admiral of the Ocean Sea .”

Columbus returned to the islands on three subsequent journeys. On the second, he dispatched a friar named Ramón Pané to live among the people of Hispaniola, record their beliefs and find strategies for converting them to Christianity.

Word soon spread that Columbus had allowed forced labor of Indigenous peoples . In 1500, he returned to Spain in chains to face charges of incompetent administration of the colonies and enslaving subjects of the realm.

Eager to get back into his patrons’ good graces – especially Isabella’s, since she was the most alarmed at his actions – he became consumed by the history and theology of the church. He studied scripture as well as the writings of prominent theologians, including St. Augustine and the 15th-century French cardinal and astrologer Pierre d'Ailly .

Like a magpie on a spiritual quest, Columbus transcribed portions from the Bible and scholars into a kind of commonplace book – a journal where he recorded parts of scripture and other writings, including his own notes. He intended the book for his queen and king, though it is likely they never saw it.

Nonetheless, their condemnation softened and they gave him permission to return to the Indies. He probably took the book along on his fourth journey of 1504. His son Ferdinand, who promoted his father’s legacy, called it the “Book of Prophecies .”

Columbus told a powerful tale in its pages . He believed that God had endowed him with remarkable intelligence, despite enemies’ allegations that he was “an uneducated man, an uninformed sailor, an ordinary person.”

Columbus compared his struggles with those of biblical prophets, saying he was like Isaiah, who “was not just a prophet, but also an evangelist” who called “all people to our holy Catholic faith.” He wrote about the discovery of islands and converting “all peoples and nations.” He reported that the Roman historian Seneca had prophesied that “a large landmass” would appear during “the last years of the world,” adding that a “new sailor” would “discover a new world.”

In this book, which was not published in his lifetime, Columbus recast the renaming and charting of Caribbean islands as a religious pursuit . He used Scripture to try to understand its geography, specifically seeking the Mount Zion mentioned in the Bible. He believed he had uncovered the Caribbean’s secrets because he had divine support for his task. The explorer wanted his royal patrons to see his role in history as something foretold by the ancients.

Columbus’ reputation has suffered over the years, with greater focus on what followed his voyages, including the spread of enslavement and environmental destruction. As one scholar put it in 1992, amid commemorations of the 500th anniversary of his first journey, the explorer was “ mugged on the way to his own party .”

In recent years, protesters have torn down his statues and splattered others with red paint. His defenders have dredged statues out of rivers and remounted them. Each side has focused on his actions and their impact rather than his writings.

In those texts, the conquest and colonization of the Western Hemisphere were inseparable from religious conversion. His actions echoed in subsequent generations, evident in other Europeans’ efforts to spread Christianity in the Americas . Catholic Iberians, English Anglicans and Puritans, and French Huguenots all latched onto that same idea: the hemisphere should become integrated into Christendom.

articles.title: What is a professional patient advocate, and why might you need one?
articles.author:
<name>Jennifer Schlinger, Clinical Associate Professor of Social Work, University of North Dakota</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jennifer-schlinger-2655258"/>
paras: Imagine your mom has just been discharged from the hospital to a rehabilitation center after hip replacement surgery. She has the paperwork, the facility’s address – and a long list of questions. Will her insurance cover her entire rehab stay? Does she have enough pain medication until she gets settled? Will the hospital transfer her prescriptions? Are they accurate?

Scenarios like this are exactly what patient advocates are trained to help with. They understand patients’ and families’ concerns, ensure their voices are heard by medical staff and interface with care teams, insurance companies and facility administrators. They also coordinate care, set up follow-up appointments and address potential gaps or blind spots in care.

I train social workers – who often serve as patient advocates – to help people in a variety of settings, including hospitals and nursing homes. Earlier in my career, I served as a professional patient advocate supporting people in hospitals, home health and hospice.
A trained patient advocate can provide much-needed support for people on their healthcare journey. Here’s what you need to know to work with one most effectively.

Patient advocacy emerged out of the Civil Rights Movement’s focus on individual protections and rights. In 1966, healthcare advocacy pioneer Ruth Ravich founded the Department of Patient Representation at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York – widely considered the beginning of the patient advocate role.

Historically, doctors made decisions for patients without fully involving them in their own care . But during the 1960s and in subsequent decades, a growing patient rights movement embraced the importance of informed consent for honoring patients’ autonomy. Patient advocates arose as an important voice in this movement by educating patients about their rights and helping them participate more fully in decisions about their healthcare.

For decades, “patient advocate” was a self-described title, not a standardized role. As the healthcare system became increasingly complicated, the need emerged for national standards on skills, ethics and best practices. In 2018, the Patient Advocate Certification Board established basic requirements for patient advocates and created a professional certification, which is the only one available for this role in the U.S.

Certification is not required to be a patient advocate, but it indicates that a person has received specific training for the role. To become certified, patient advocates must pass an exam demonstrating a knowledge of health and medical concepts, issues relating to paying for care, an understanding of the healthcare system, how to work collaboratively with patients and other areas of competency. They must complete continuing education to maintain certification.

Some healthcare professionals who serve as patient advocates are not certified and instead have learned relevant skills through their education or professional experiences. They may work in rural healthcare facilities, for instance, where they wear multiple hats as nurses or social workers who are also advocates.

Patient advocates are trained to support, inform and guide patients through the healthcare system. They help explain medical information, such as a medication’s side effects or treatment options. They also make sure patients’ questions are answered and their concerns are addressed.

When a patient receives a referral to a specialist, a patient advocate can connect care across various healthcare providers, making sure details about the patient’s condition or care priorities don’t fall through the cracks and helping to arrange transportation to appointments.

Early in my career, for instance, I worked at a hospital with patients who were being discharged to their home or to a long-term care facility. I started by understanding each patient’s goals, assessing their living arrangements and the type of care they needed and identifying any concerns they had about their discharge plan. Before they left the hospital, I coordinated community supports or additional care they might need, such as home-delivered meals, home healthcare, and physical, occupational or speech therapy.

Patients often have family members who are advocating on their behalf – and family support is invaluable . Working with a patient advocate can provide something different: a grounded, objective perspective, expert knowledge of the healthcare system and knowledge of resources that patients and family members may not be aware of.

Indeed, patient advocates interact closely with family members and friends who are involved in the patient’s care. As liaisons between the patient, family and healthcare providers, their job is to keep the patient’s needs, preferences, goals and values at the center of their care.

Working with a patient advocate can help patients feel more confident in making informed decisions. According to a 2023 survey by a nonprofit alliance called the Coalition of Healthcare Advocacy , 92% of patients and healthcare providers reported that working with a patient advocate positively affected patients’ care .

Managing financial aspects of healthcare can be overwhelming for patients and family members, particularly in the midst of a health crisis. Medical bills are often impenetrable documents littered with complex codes and terminology, and sorting through charges and details about insurance coverage can feel intimidating, if not downright paralyzing.
A patient advocate can provide a knowledgeable outside perspective on these issues that’s not clouded by the urgency and emotional weight of illness.

Some patient advocates have specialized knowledge in medical billing, coding, insurance and other financial matters. They can answer questions about medical terms or clarify charges on a patient’s bill, review the bill for errors such as incorrect or duplicate charges and assist with figuring out insurance coverage and reimbursement.

If necessary, they can also appeal claims by acting as a liaison between the patient, the healthcare facility and the insurance company. Patient advocates can also help patients work with a hospital to set up a payment plan, explore additional financial support or coordinate access to community resources.
If a finance-related question falls outside an advocate’s knowledge or expertise, they can help the patient identify the right people to talk to.
Finding a patient advocate is not always as straightforward as it should be.

If you are unsure where to start, ask to speak with a hospital social worker or case manager. In some cases, an advocate’s services are provided by the healthcare organization or are covered by insurance, but in others, the patient or family must pay for them out-of-pocket.

Many healthcare facilities, including Veterans Affairs, have patient advocates on staff. You can contact your local hospital or clinic and ask to be connected to their patient advocate. Alternatively, you can search for a patient advocate in your area through the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services website or the National Association of Healthcare Advocacy .

If a certified patient advocate is not available within your healthcare facility, request to speak with a social worker. Social workers have the education and expertise to support patients and families, to connect them with resources and to advocate for patients’ needs.

Before meeting with a patient advocate, identify your main objectives – for example, preparing for a transition home, clarifying a treatment plan or understanding medication changes. Then, write down your main concerns and questions. The Care Partner Project offers checklists for questions to ask healthcare providers, prepare for doctor visits, evaluate senior living communities and more. Gather any relevant information, such as medication lists, medical records, insurance documents and medical bills.

When you meet a patient advocate you’re considering working with, you can feel out whether they are a good fit by asking about their professional background, areas of expertise, experience and credentials. Some questions you might start with include:
What is your experience with cases like mine? (For example, patients being transferred to a rehabilitation center, if that is your situation.)
Can you provide an example of how you helped a patient or family work though a difficult healthcare situation?
How do you typically communicate with patients and families, and how often can I expect to hear from you?
How do you help patients speak up about their concerns and preferences to their healthcare providers?
Finding a healthcare advocate you trust can make navigating a complex health situation much less overwhelming.
