articles.title: Why people keep looking for Noah’s Ark in a natural rock formation in Turkey: A scholar of early Christianity explains
articles.author:
<name>Eric Vanden Eykel, Associate Professor of Religious Studies, Ferrum College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/eric-vanden-eykel-1187893"/>
paras: A team of researchers from Sivas Cumhuriyet University in Turkey is investigating a long-standing claim: that a boat-shaped geological formation in the country’s east contains the remains of Noah’s Ark.

In the biblical Book of Genesis , God decides to destroy the world with a flood. Following God’s instructions, Noah builds an ark – a large wooden vessel – to save himself, his family and animals of every kind.

The formation in question, known as Durupınar, has been associated with Noah’s Ark for nearly 70 years. This new research team has attracted social media attention through a partnership with a separate U.S.-based Christian organization called Noah’s Ark Scans . This group has promoted the Durupınar site as the resting place of Noah’s Ark since at least 2021.
Durupınar is a natural geological formation composed of sedimentary material rich in iron oxides. It is located near the town of Doğubayazıt , just a few miles from the Iranian border.

Official statements from researchers involved in this project say that laboratory analysis is still underway. Researchers have nevertheless described some preliminary findings as potentially consistent with a shiplike structure, while claims circulating on social media have been more definitive, saying that scans have confirmed the formation is man-made and “100% not geological.”
Claims that the formation is man-made have also appeared in British and American media coverage .

As a scholar of early Christianity , I study biblical texts and their interpretation. Certain claims about the Durupınar formation have been circulating for decades, and they offer an opportunity to examine how people read and interpret the biblical flood story.
To understand the current claims, it helps to ask how this formation came to be associated with Noah’s Ark in the first place.

The Durupınar formation takes its name from the Turkish Army captain İlhan Durupınar, who noticed the formation’s boatlike shape while examining aerial photographs of the region in 1959. Because of its close proximity to a peak known since the Middle Ages as Mount Ararat, which the Genesis flood account claims is the place that Noah’s Ark came to rest , Durupınar wondered whether this formation might be the petrified remains of the ark, preserved in the landscape over time.

The following year, Durupınar joined a team sponsored by the Archaeological Research Foundation in the United States on an expedition to the site. Led by George Vandeman, a television evangelist, and Arthur Brandenberger, a specialist who used aerial photographs to measure and map the landscape , the team traveled to the site with the explicit goal of confirming whether it was, in fact, the petrified remains of the fabled Ark of Noah.

The expedition was the subject of a short article in the Sept. 5, 1960, issue of LIFE magazine . The article noted that while one member of the expedition remained skeptical on whether nature alone could be responsible for a shape like this, the surveys conducted ultimately “revealed no sign that the object was man made.” The expedition therefore concluded that it was a natural geological formation. In other words, it wasn’t the petrified remains of the biblical Noah’s Ark.

In the wake of the 1960 expedition, interest in Durupınar waned, and the case was closed for a time. The site returned to public attention in the late 1970s, when Ron Wyatt , a nurse anesthetist and amateur archaeologist inspired by the LIFE article, traveled to Durupınar to investigate for himself.

While at the site, Wyatt conducted a series of tests and eventually claimed that the formation was actually the remains of Noah’s Ark. He argued that radar and other scans showed evidence of walls, decks, petrified wood, metal fittings and other materials that one might expect to find in the ruins of a wooden ship. Wyatt was also intrigued by large stones near the site that he claimed would have hung from the boat and steadied it while it was afloat.

Wyatt was initially able to convince another amateur archaeologist from the U.S., David Fasold, that his claims were true. In fact, in 1988 Fasold published a book in which he argued that the Durupınar formation was Noah’s Ark.

Fasold’s enthusiasm for the site was relatively short-lived, however, and not even 10 years after publishing his book on the topic he co-authored a journal article with geologist Lorence Collins that overturned his earlier conclusions. After a full assessment of the available evidence, Fasold concluded that “the supposed Ark near [Doğubayazıt] is a completely natural rock formation. It cannot have been Noah’s Ark nor even a man-made model.”

Trained geologists have tended to agree with the assessment of Fasold and Collins: Durupınar is a natural geological formation rather than the remains of a wooden ship. Geologist Murat Avcı, for example, identifies the boat-shaped feature as a large block of limestone that moved downslope in a landslide and was subsequently shaped by an earthflow and other geological processes .

Geological analyses identified the material that Wyatt described as petrified wood as ordinary rock , and the objects described as iron brackets as weathered volcanic material. The patterns that were interpreted as compartments of the ark are consistent with the formation’s natural structure and fracturing , while the proposed “anchor stones” are actually made of local volcanic rock.

All of the results from the most recent research project are, at the moment, still preliminary and inconclusive . Samples are waiting to be analyzed in labs, and official communications from the university say that evaluation of the evidence will continue into 2027.
As a biblical scholar, though, I am more interested in our ongoing fascination with flood stories.

Most biblical scholars read the story of the flood in Genesis as part of a much older tradition of flood mythology from the ancient Near East. Writers in ancient Mesopotamia told several versions of a story in which the gods send a catastrophic flood but warn one man, who then builds a large boat to save his family and animals.

In the Atrahasis Epic , for example, known from manuscripts dating back to the second millennium B.C.E., that survivor is Atrahasis. Another version of the same story also appears in the Epic of Gilgamesh , where the flood survivor Utnapishtim builds a large boat to weather the storm.

Genesis does not simply copy these older stories; it reshapes them. In Atrahasis, noisy humans become annoying to the gods, so the gods drown them. Genesis, on the other hand, presents violence and corruption as the chief problem . The ending of Genesis also moves in a different direction. Rather than imposing new limits on human reproduction, as the Atrahasis epic does, God in Genesis blesses Noah’s family, tells them to “be fruitful and multiply,” and establishes a covenant with all of humankind and every living creature .

One of the more interesting things about the flood story in Genesis is that the flood actually fails to solve the problem that caused it in the first place. Before the flood, humankind is inclined toward evil. After the flood, the problem is still there . But the story isn’t ultimately about eliminating human wickedness; it is about how life goes on despite humankind’s enduring flaws.

The current search at Durupınar, like those that came before it, assumes that behind the biblical story there is tangible evidence just waiting to be found. For nearly 70 years this boat-shaped formation has kept that possibility alive.

Ancient flood stories and how they changed across cultures can reveal how people made sense of catastrophe, human violence and the possibility of starting over. A boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey probably cannot.

articles.title: Does your sleep tracker get it right? A Pittsburgh neuroscientist weighs in
articles.author:
<name>J. David Creswell, Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience, Carnegie Mellon University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/j-david-creswell-2372977"/>
paras: On a typical night, I go to bed wearing a tracking watch on one wrist and another type of tracker on the other wrist. Then I compare their sleep findings while I drink my morning coffee.

I direct the Center for Modern Digital Health at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, where my team and I study how to use wearables to improve health and performance. My lab’s research has relied on consumer devices for years. I wear them for both science and pleasure, and I also wonder how much of what they tell me is true.

Apple’s newest watch , announced Sept. 9, 2026, greets its wearers each morning with a single “readiness” number, built partly from how it thinks they slept. Apple says the redesigned sensors deliver the most accurate heart-rate tracking of any wearable, but independent labs have not yet confirmed that.
Given the growing popularity of sleep trackers, I think it’s worth asking whether a sensor on your wrist or finger can really tell you how your brain was sleeping last night.
Here’s what recent studies show when consumer wearables are tested against the gold standard, polysomnography .
Polysomnography, which combines EEG, or electroencephalogram , with other sensors, records brain waves, eye movements and muscle tone while a person sleeps.

On the simplest question – asleep or awake – today’s devices come close. A 2025 meta-analysis of 24 studies and nearly 800 participants found that wearables typically overestimate total sleep time by about 17 minutes compared with polysomnography. In an eight-hour night, that’s an error of under 4%, roughly two taps of the snooze button.

That gap comes from a blind spot every wearable shares: quiet wakefulness. When you lie awake motionless in the dark, your tracker often mistakes it for sleep. If you sleep well, that rarely matters, because you don’t spend much time lying awake. But if you have insomnia, those long, still stretches add up, and your wearable is probably overestimating how much sleep you’re getting.

I will start with the obvious: That wearable on your arm or finger does not measure your brain. It measures your heart rate, the beat-to-beat variability of that heart rate, your movement and your skin temperature. The bet the wearable companies are making is that the different sleep stages we go through at night leave trace fingerprints on all of these – REM sleep , for instance, has a distinctive cardiovascular profile – and the wearable’s algorithm reads those sleep fingerprints and makes an educated guess about which stage you are in.

How good is that guess? A 2025 study of six wrist devices worn by 62 adults found only modest agreement with polysomnography on sleep stages, along with significant gaps on time awake after falling asleep and on sleep efficiency. The authors concluded the better-performing watches could track “prolonged and significant changes in sleep architecture.”
Translation: Your deep-sleep number is a noisy nightly estimate, best used to identify significant changes in your sleep over time.

One of my lab’s findings comes from using these devices for what they’re good at. In a 2023 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, we used Fitbits to track the sleep of more than 600 first-year students at three universities, including Carnegie Mellon University. We found that a student sleeping six or fewer hours a night early in the semester had a lower end of term grade-point average relative to their previous semester – an effect that held even after we accounted for academic load and daytime naps.
Nightly sleep duration is the number these devices track well, and it’s the one my students can actually do something about, mostly by getting to bed earlier.

In a 2023 randomized trial , 113 adults with insomnia symptoms spent five weeks in one of two groups. One group got feedback on their sleep as measured by a wearable sensor, along with guidance on how to interpret it. The other got standard sleep-hygiene education: general advice on habits such as keeping a regular bedtime, cutting back on caffeine and screens, and keeping the bedroom dark and quiet.

The feedback group ended up reporting milder insomnia symptoms than the sleep-hygiene group, but the measured amount of sleep they were getting was unchanged. They weren’t sleeping longer, falling asleep faster or waking less. The researchers expected the data to correct a common pattern in insomnia: People often report sleeping less than the sensors record. The feedback didn’t shrink that gap any more than the sleep-hygiene sessions did. What changed was how troubled people felt about their sleep: The feedback group ended up less troubled by it, even though the sleep itself stayed the same.

That distinction between measured sleep and felt sleep is one that sleep scientists here in Pittsburgh have shaped for decades. Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh developed the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index in 1989, a questionnaire that asks people to rate how they slept rather than measuring it with wearables. It remains one of the most widely used sleep measures in the world.
The trial’s results suggest that for many people, a wearable’s biggest effect is on the score that the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index measures: subjective feelings of one’s sleep quality.

A 2026 trial of 229 older adults in Japan points the same way . Everyone got regular reports from a sleep monitor placed under their bedding. Participants who got the reports alone saw no improvement in their insomnia scores, but those who also got monthly phone guidance on sleep habits and daytime activity did, at least over the first three months. As in the first study, what improved was how people rated their sleep.
A wearable can tell you how much you slept; it can’t make you sleep more. That part is up to you, or to someone who helps you.

And for some people, the tracking itself becomes the problem. Sleep clinicians have a name for patients who lie awake worrying about their sleep score: orthosomnia , a term coined in 2017 and still very much in use . If checking your score reliably wrecks your morning, the device isn’t working for you.

I read the sleep stages and readiness scores the way I read a weather forecast: a useful trend but a poor guide to any single night. And I keep in mind that by the time a study comes out, the device it tested has often been replaced .

paras: The last 2026 primary elections were held on Sept. 15 in Delaware . Although totals are not yet available, there is evidence that turnout was higher than in most prior election years.

This year’s primaries were also the most competitive in recent history; 13 congressional incumbents were defeated, the largest number since the 1950s other than the years when redistricting forced some incumbents to run against each other.

Primary competition is often a predictor of general election competition . In wave election years, as this year is expected to be, the party that gains seats in Congress often had more competitive primaries, a consequence of the increase in candidates seeking nomination and the enthusiasm of voters. This year, that competition bodes well for Democrats.

The story the 2026 primaries tell about democracy, however, is less rosy. The 2026 primaries were held on 21 dates , from March to September. State turnout levels varied substantially , and in many states it appears that politically moderate voters stayed home . Some states, such as Maine and Michigan, had heated battles in marquee races, while other states, such as Connecticut, had virtually no competition.

From my perspective as a political scientist , each of these facts represents a problem for democracy. If the purpose of primaries is to allow each party’s voters an opportunity to choose candidates, the 2026 primaries – like primaries in most years – did not achieve those goals. In fact, their outcomes represented the views of a small group of people who turn out inconsistently and often do not even represent the views of the parties’ voters, to say nothing of the general public.
My recent book, “ The Problem with Primary Voters ,” co-authored with Caroline Tolbert and Nathan Micatka, documents these problems. Here they are, and how they undermine democracy.
In the past three midterm elections – 2014, 2018 and 2022 – primary turnout averaged approximately 20% of the voting age population .

Turnout varies according to competition at the state level, state primary rules and state political culture. Western states such as Montana and Washington average slightly over 30% turnout, while Connecticut, New York and Virginia average less than 10%.
Because so few general election races are competitive, a tiny sliver of voters effectively choose most of Congress through their votes in the primary.
If primary voters looked like everyone else, low turnout might not be a problem. But they don’t.

They are much older, somewhat better educated, less racially diverse and wealthier than other eligible voters. Most importantly, the representativeness of primary voters does not increase when primary turnout goes up.

In Massachusetts, for instance, turnout increased by half from 2014 to 2022 – from 14% to 21% of the voting age population . Yet turnout among the very wealthy more than doubled, while turnout among the least wealthy actually decreased, leaving the electorate less representative, by income, in 2022 than it had been in 2014 .
We studied data about more than 3 million American voters for our book. We found that fewer than half of primary voters in any given year voted in the primary four years earlier.

This creates a problem of representation, and this lack of consistency, we found, is a particular challenge for U.S. House or state legislative candidates: They cannot know who will actually show up in the primary. And even if they try to represent their party’s voters, the voters who show up are unlikely to be there because of them.

In 2026 this problem was made worse by the mid-decade redistricting prompted by the Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais decision , along with the decisions by governors in Louisiana and Alabama to postpone their states’ primaries. No one has studied voter awareness of primary dates, but surely many eligible voters do not know when their states’ primaries are held, especially in states without a competitive primary for governor or U.S. Senate, or where dates have recently changed.
Low primary turnout can also lead to unexpected results – and these results can create misleading perceptions of the election.

In 2026, for instance, upset victories by Democratic Socialist candidates in New York, with an 11% turnout, and Colorado, with a 34% turnout, led to a spate of news stories about the success of socialists. But these candidates’ victories were the result of small shifts in particular districts, not major changes in the Democratic electorate.
Many reform advocates who are concerned about political extremism have proposed changing primary election laws.

The reforms include adopting a top-two nonpartisan primary , such as those in California and Washington, or a top-four nonpartisan primary with a ranked-choice general election , as is used in Alaska . In each of these cases, a specific number of candidates chosen in a nonpartisan primary go on to the general election.
Others have proposed mandating open primaries , where any voter can request the ballot of either party.
These reforms can have targeted, albeit limited, effects – they can increase competition in lopsidedly partisan districts and give members of the minority party more of a voice.

However, these reforms are unlikely to solve the turnout problem. Increasing turnout by 5 percentage points or so will not necessarily make the electorate more representative or encourage people to vote more consistently.

To increase the participation, representation and consistency of primary voters, I believe it is necessary to consolidate primary dates. One way to do this would be to establish a national primary day . If all states voted on the same day, we expect turnout would increase in part because people would know when to vote, and those who vote based on a sense of duty, as opposed to partisanship, would be more likely to show up.
If this seems too far-fetched, reformers could still push states to consolidate their primaries on fewer days – to create a set of regional primaries.

Some scholars have argued that political parties should exert more control over nominations, and that strong parties may not need the input of voters in order to offer voters clear and responsible choices about public policies.

It is true that most democratic countries do not use primaries at all. Yet there is no chance that America will get rid of primaries any time soon. If we are going to have them, and they are to fulfill their purpose, it is important that they be predictable – that politicians know who the voters will be and that the voters look like the population.
Otherwise voters, nonvoters and politicians risk learning the wrong lessons from the primaries.

articles.title: Why older lawmakers may wait too long to step aside
articles.author:
<name>Nancy Forster-Holt, Clinical Associate Professor of Innovation and Entrepreneurship, University of Rhode Island</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/nancy-forster-holt-1545758"/>
paras: U.S. Sen. Ed Markey is 80 and has served in Congress for half a century . His Democratic primary challenger in Massachusetts, U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, is 47 and made generational change a centerpiece of his campaign. Markey won the Sept. 1, 2026, primary anyway by nearly 30 percentage points.

He’s not the only octogenarian to prevail in a competitive primary in 2026. Eleven won their primaries and are on the ballot for the 2026 midterm elections . The oldest primary winner was Sen. Jim Risch of Idaho, an 83-year-old Republican.
It seems to be an issue both major political parties agree on: For many candidates, age is just a number, even when it starts with an 8 or a 9.

My colleagues and I study succession in family-run businesses and other occupations where leadership, identity and longevity can become deeply intertwined. Whether someone is in charge of a company or is a lawmaker, their work does not only keep them busy. It provides status, an identity and a sense of mission. Letting go means giving up more than a job.
When business leaders or politicians linger for too long , it can be costly for their companies or constituents because potential successors may become frustrated by waiting and decide to move on.

When any kind of leader remains in their role for decades, underlying reasons can range from a genuine love for what they do to not knowing what they will do – or who they will be – once they leave. However, waiting too long can mean they’ll have to hand off their responsibilities in crisis mode.
In family businesses, my research team found, the people closest to their leaders – including relatives, employees and longtime supporters – may go quiet rather than press the issue .
This dynamic is not limited to the business world. It also applies to many of the older members of Congress.
A closer look at the large numbers of legislators who continue to serve during their golden years reflects two trends.
First, many are elected for the first time when they’re middle-aged. New House members were about 50 years old and new senators around 55 in 2025.

Second, although the median age of House lawmakers is now about 60 , and 66 in the Senate , there’s a small group of long-serving members who remain in office into and past their 80s and keep running for reelection.
Every lawmaker can have a reason to say “not yet.” So can their staff members, who may be loyal to them and their missions and professionally invested in the work they have built together.

Political parties value the electoral advantages of incumbents, while constituents may value the seniority, relationships and influence that come with having spent decades serving in Congress . And incumbents can sincerely believe important work remains unfinished .
However, unusually prolonged service in any position increases the possibility that illness, cognitive decline or death will lead to an unplanned and probably rocky transition.
What’s more, when politicians serve into their late 70s, 80s or beyond, they are breaking with ordinary employment patterns.
The typical American retires in their early 60s , with two-thirds of U.S. workers exiting the labor force before their 65th birthday.
There are examples of long-serving politicians choosing to plan their exit closer to standard retirement age.

One is Barbara Boxer. After more than three decades in Congress, the 74-year-old California Democrat announced in January 2015 that she would not seek reelection to the U.S. Senate the following year. “There is a time when you want the next generation to step in and step up,” she said.

Boxer’s early decision gave prospective successors nearly two years to organize and voters the opportunity to choose among them. Kamala Harris won the seat but stepped away to serve as President Joe Biden’s vice president.

This departure offers a striking contrast with that of Boxer’s longtime colleague, Sen. Dianne Feinstein, who remained in the Senate through a lengthy health-related absence in 2023. Feinstein, also a California Democrat, died in office that September. She was 90 years old.

She served on the influential Senate Judiciary Committee , which considers federal judicial nominations, including Supreme Court nominees. During her nearly three-month absence, the committee was deadlocked on dozens of Biden nominations after Republicans refused to let the Democrats appoint a temporary replacement for her and she refused to step down.
The tragic way Feinstein’s storied political career ended illustrated what can go wrong when lawmakers keep saying “not yet” until it’s too late .

That turned out to be the case with Biden, who reluctantly ended his presidential reelection campaign in July 2024 . However, several books published since then include details about how his inner circle initially advised him to run again .
A rushed attempt at succession followed Biden’s abrupt withdrawal from the race. Harris became the Democratic nominee without participating in any of the 2024 primaries.
When change finally came, it arrived under duress rather than by design. And Harris lost the election to Donald Trump.

U.S. Rep. Kay Granger, a Texas Republican, announced in 2023 that she would not seek reelection the following year. It soon became clear that severe health problems were preventing her from serving her constituents.

The former House Appropriations Committee chair didn’t cast a vote in her final six months in office for a good reason: She had dementia and was staying in a Texas assisted-living facility that provided memory care services to some residents. Granger died in August 2026 at 83 .

U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, a former Senate majority and minority leader, has announced that he will step down when his current term – the Kentucky Republican’s seventh – ends in January 2027. But a fall, hospitalization and subsequent stint in a rehabilitation center in mid-2026 prompted renewed public scrutiny of the 84-year-old’s health and ability to complete his term.

U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, who turned 93 on Sept. 17, 2026 , and appears to be in good health, has not yet said whether he’s running for a ninth six-year term in 2028. But the Republican, who is the oldest person serving in Congress, has urged his constituents to vote for a Republican for governor.
“I don’t plan on dying in office, but if I did, I don’t want a Democratic governor choosing my successor,” Grassley said at a political event in Des Moines in late September 2026.
My colleagues and I found an unlikely way to think differently about leadership transitions: considering lessons about letting go from palliative care.

Leaving political office or another leadership role, of course, is not the same as dying. But, as is true before someone develops a terminal medical condition, advance planning is most useful while people can still articulate what matters to them and exercise meaningful choices about what comes next.

I’ve learned that it’s a mistake to treat succession as something to discuss only when a leader must move on for health or other reasons. So, in addition to my work as a management professor, and to inform my research, as well as the workshops I hold for aging business owners and members of their inner circles, I have been trained as an end-of-life doula . I decided to do this because I lacked the vocabulary and tools that facilitated difficult conversations and decisions about their legacy and what is important to the leader as they let go.
Palliative care supports the act of letting go long before death – the same challenge confronting business leaders and the companies they run.

When voters consider whether to vote for an aging incumbent, they may wonder whether that lawmaker is already too old for their demanding job or soon will be. But that may be the wrong question. It might be better to ask whether the legislators who represent you, no matter their age, have a plan for letting go.

Nancy Forster-Holt does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Amazon hires a veteran Microsoft AI leader to help build its tools for coding and work
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: A longtime Microsoft engineering leader who was previously a Copilot chief technology officer is joining Amazon Web Services to work on its competing AI tools for coding and workplace productivity.

Pedram Rezaei , a nearly 20-year Microsoft veteran who was most recently a corporate vice president on the Microsoft Superintelligence team, starts Monday as a distinguished engineer in the AWS Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies organization, led by Swami Sivasubramanian.

Rezaei will work initially on Kiro, the AWS coding tool, and Quick, Amazon’s AI assistant for workplace tasks, Sivasubramanian wrote in a memo to his team Monday. “He is a hands-on engineer who is still in the code every day, and he plans to keep it that way here,” he added.

Kiro’s user count doubled from the first quarter to the second, and monthly AI users for Quick grew fourfold, according to the memo. Rezaei’s plan for his first few months is to “meet people, learn how things work here, and ship something real,” Sivasubramanian wrote.
Sivasubramanian’s organization was expanded in July to include emerging technologies, part of a broader reshuffling of Amazon’s AI teams.

The hire comes as Amazon and Microsoft compete more directly in AI tools for work. Microsoft last month unveiled an all-in-one Copilot app that combines chat, coding and agents, its answer to OpenAI and Anthropic. Amazon made its Quick desktop app generally available in September and brought its main features to mobile.

Rezaei joined Microsoft in 2006 and held senior technical roles on Power BI, Dynamics 365, Cortana, Bing and Azure Maps before moving to Copilot, according to his LinkedIn profile . He became Copilot’s CTO in February and moved to the Microsoft Superintelligence team in June, according to the profile. Sivasubramanian’s memo said Rezaei was most recently working on training foundation models.
We’ve contacted Microsoft for comment on his departure.
Rezaei is the latest Microsoft executive to move to AWS this year. Shawn Bice returned to AWS in May from a security role at Microsoft to lead its Automated Reasoning Group.

In his memo Monday, Sivasubramanian also told his team that two longtime AWS engineers, Marvin Theimer and Reto Kramer , have returned to work on neurosymbolic AI and automated reasoning, which he called “one of our biggest bets for the future.” Both came back from Microsoft, according to their LinkedIn profiles.
Neurosymbolic AI pairs large language models with rule-based systems that can check whether an AI agent is following a company’s policies and procedures.

Speaking at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in Seattle last week, Sivasubramanian said nearly every CIO and CEO raises the same question about AI agents. “How do I know it is always going to obey all my rules and regulations?” he said. “This is a real concern.”
Solving that problem “actually unlocks so many use cases for all these enterprises,” he added.

Theimer, an AWS distinguished engineer for nine years before leaving in 2022, joined Microsoft in July 2024 as a corporate vice president and technical architect and stayed until March. It was his second stint at the company, where he worked from 1998 to 2006. He rejoined AWS in July as a vice president and distinguished engineer.

Kramer, who led an automated reasoning team at AWS before leaving in 2023, joined Microsoft in September 2025 as vice president of Security Platform & AI and stayed until May. He rejoined AWS in September as vice president of applied science.
Sivasubramanian hinted at more hires to come, writing that Rezaei joins “as we continue to build out our technical leadership team to help take on the ambitious work we have planned.”

articles.title: Seattle’s tax burden shifted to business as jobs slipped away, new report finds
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Seattle’s tax collections have nearly tripled over the past decade, soaring from $900 million in 2013 to a projected $2.8 billion in 2026. But who pays those taxes, and how the tax revenue is collected, looks vastly different today than a decade ago.

A new report released by ECOnorthwest, commissioned jointly by the Downtown Seattle Association (DSA) and the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, show city tax revenues far outstripping population and job growth, driven by targeted corporate taxes on a small pool of major employers.

Between 2013 and 2025, Seattle’s tax revenues jumped 172%, outpacing population growth (31%), job growth (23%), and local inflation (50%) . During that period, real tax growth grew 5.6 times faster than population and 7.5 times faster than employment .

The findings come as city leaders, major tech employers and regional business groups grapple with shifting post-pandemic work patterns and a political climate that has frequently placed large technology companies like Amazon in its sights.

According to the report, broad-based core taxes, such as property, sales, utility, and general Business & Occupation (B&O) taxes, comprised 83% of city tax collections in 2013. By 2026, those core broad taxes are projected to drop to just 52% of the total revenue.
Replacing them are narrow, targeted tax levies :

Combined, two taxes that did not exist five years ago now account for nearly a third of all business tax dollars collected by the city. Overlap among top taxpayers means fewer than 20 companies account for roughly $356 million in annual City of Seattle revenue.

“Seattle’s tax collections are growing far faster than its population, jobs or inflation. Employers are carrying more of that burden. That trajectory is not sustainable,” said Seattle Metro Chamber president & CEO Joe Nguyen. “The question cannot always be how to collect more money. It must be how to deliver better results with the money we already have and build a tax structure that helps our economy grow.”
The heavy pivot to business revenue coincides with divergent employment trends between Seattle and its neighboring Eastside hubs .

Between March 2020 and March 2025, Seattle lost approximately 24,000 jobs, while the remainder of King County added 21,000. The report notes that Seattle lost 18,000 jobs in the single year leading up to March 2025 alone. And that figure that does not yet capture the full impact of major remote work policies and tech layoffs announced across the region.

The report arrives on the heels of previous GeekWire coverage tracking regional tech dynamics, including the shift of high tech jobs from Seattle to Bellevue , as well as broader political shifts in how West Coast hubs are responding to tech sector backlash and the AI boom .

However, in a sign that Mayor Katie Wilson is paying close attention to tech-sector headwinds and shifting job patterns, she proposed a $9.1 billion 2027 budget that would erase a $175 million general fund deficit and cut nearly $50 million in spending while freezing JumpStart tax rates.

articles.title: Ballard Link Community Forum on October 19
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Seattle City Councilmember (District 6) and Sound Transit Boardmember Dan Strauss is hosting a community form discussing the Ballard Link Extension alongside several other elected officials and Sound Transit representatives. The forum will be held in the Osberg Great Hall at the National Nordic Museum on Monday, October 19, from 6-8pm .

In a newsletter emailed to constituents last week, Dan Strauss announced the event while highlighting his efforts to get Sound Transit to commit to building the full Ballard Link Extension to Market Street. These included requiring Sound Transit staff to determine when the agency would be able to complete the Ballard Link Extension under current conditions, and looking for ways to reduce project costs in order to open the extension sooner. Currently, the agency expects to open the SODO to Seattle Center portion of the Ballard Link Extension in 2042.

In July, Sound Transit fulfilled Strauss’ first requirement with the announcement the rest of the project could be delayed to 2060 unless significant cost savings are found. When voters passed ST3 in 2016, the entire Ballard Link Extension was expected to open in 2035. In 2021, this schedule slipped to 2037 or 2039 as Sound Transit realized the cost to build a second Link-only tunnel under downtown and managing other complications would far exceed expectations . After calculating “bottom-up” cost estimates for the proposed design of the extension last year, the agency found the full project could cost nearly twice its previous estimate. Compounded with exploding cost estimates across ST3, the Sound Transit Board voted to defer construction of line past Seattle Center until costs were reduced or additional revenue were found.

Sound Transit says it may be able to open the full extension in 2042 if the agency can reduce the total estimated cost by $1 billion (or identify that much in new revenue), begin acquiring property by 2030, finish design by 2032, and lock in funding to start construction by 2033. Regardless, Ballard Link advocates remain dedicated to pushing Sound Transit to return to the originally promised date of opening in 2035.

At the community forum, Sound Transit is expected to share more about its proposed timeline for the Ballard Link Extension, the work agency staff have been doing to reduce costs, and its next steps for the project. There will also be a Q&A session.

Those interested in a seat should probably arrive early. The National Nordic Museum is located at the intersection of 28th Ave NW and NW Market Street, just under a mile west of the planned terminus of the Ballard Link Extension. Nearby bus stops are served by King County Metro Routes 17 and 44 .

articles.title: Deadline Approaches for Outside Ideas to Curb Costs on Ballard Light Rail
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: The due date is approaching for engineering firms to submit cost-saving ideas for the Ballard Link light rail extension, but some transit advocates are criticizing Sound Transit's process and questioning whether the agency is actually open to new ideas and innovative approaches.

Many Sound Transit 3 (ST3) expansion projects are facing headwinds, but Ballard Link in particular faces considerable uncertainty, with a 2042 opening date for the whole line the best case scenario, which would require closing a huge budget gap of around $8 billion. The less-rosy scenario would be opening only the portion through Downtown Seattle in the 2040s and delaying the Interbay and Ballard section to the 2060s , allowing more time for funding to accrue in Sound Transit's coffers. West Seattle Link, meanwhile, has slipped to 2035 – five years later than initially envisioned.

When the Sound Transit Board of Directors overhauled project schedules on May 28, it established a Request for Information (RFI) process to solicit cost-effective design ideas for Ballard Link from outside firms. However that RFI didn't actually go out the door until last month. Sound Transit issued the RFI on September 2, with responses due October 5. That deadline has since been extended a week to October 12.

Advocates with the Save Ballard Rail coalition pushed for the RFI and hoped that it would open the door to much more cost-effective approaches that allow Sound Transit to deliver light rail to Ballard closer to its original timeline in the 2030s.

One of those cost-slashing ideas was converting Ballard Link to an automated light rail (ALR) system with shorter trains and stations, as proposed in a white paper by former Seattle Department of Transportation director Scott Kubly and transportation planner Trevor Reed, and popularized in an Urbanist op-ed . Copenhagen used this technology to overcome their own financial crisis and deliver a highly successful metro system, providing a proof of concept, but the authors do not think Sound Transit is taking their idea seriously.

"They have structured an RFI process that is almost guaranteed to validate their current approach," Kubly and Reed told The Urbanist in a joint written response. "They did no industry outreach ahead of time, they barely publicized the RFI, and they gave an extremely abbreviated response period. This is not the approach of a competent agency or an agency that wants serious responses. This is a clear example of a bureaucratic following the letter but not the spirit of a board request."

Another idea that has garnered interest from Save Ballard Rail and other transit groups is exploring elevated rail as a means to avoid incurring huge costs digging a deep tunnel and cavernous stations in downtown Seattle. Civil engineer Travis Henderson pitched the idea in a white paper he sent to Sound Transit this spring and finetuned in an op-ed in The Urbanist last month. Several transit groups endorsed studying the idea, including Seattle Subway and Transit Equity for All.

"Against a 34-year wait until 2060 for the full line, two or three years of further study is not the risk. The current plan is," Henderson wrote. "Declining to study an alternative with $10 billion in potential savings because the analysis may cost tens of millions is not sound process management. It is institutional inertia, a sunk-cost fallacy that completes the paperwork for a tunnel Sound Transit cannot afford to build, while blocking the alternatives most likely to reach Ballard."

Henderson pointed out the parameters of the RFI precluded firms from putting forward elevated rail as a replacement for planned tunnel sections downtown. The RFI instructs respondents that they "must be mindful of the existing project definition and eschew strategies that could further jeopardize the project timeline." Since Sound Transit has never formally studied elevated rail for the downtown section, it does not fit the project definition.
In a series of Bluesky posts , Kubly criticized how quietly Sound Transit was conducting the RFI process.

"Thursday before Labor Day they issue [the RFI], wait 1.5 weeks to publicize, give 30 days to respond," Kubly wrote. "It’s almost as if they don’t want serious responses. Their staff wrote a memo in April reviewing our proposal. Tips their hand that they aren’t receptive to new ideas."

Kubly also questioned whether agency staff had given automated light rail proposal a fair shot. Sound Transit's deputy executive director for enterprise planning, Alex Krieg, quietly issued an internal memo responding to Kubly and Reed's proposal in April, but the agency didn't send it to the authors or the outside world until June 12 – after the board had voted on the financial plan.

The memo poo-poos the savings possible with shorter choo choos, claiming Kubly and Reed overestimated how large planned stations are likely to be. Additionally, Krieg argued Seattle costs are uniquely driven up by high seismic risk and the earthquake-proofing requirements that brings related to liquefaction risk and unfavorable soil conditions (trouble spots are composed of loose glacial till or man-made fill) and routing obstacles that would still be in play with shorter stations.

"While having shorter station platforms would make station-siting easier, tunnel and station depths on Ballard Link are driven primarily by the need to route around and below existing building foundations, construction tiebacks, and major utilities – not by station size," Krieg wrote in the memo. "The depth of Westlake Station, for example, is set by the need to tunnel under the foundation caissons of the Motif Hotel. These constraints exist regardless of vehicle technology or station size."

It's interesting that the agency is considering a hotel built in 1973 an immutable obstacle. Motif last sold for $145 million in February 2018 – although the 19-story tower did see a renovation in 2023, according to Puget Sound Business Journal . It's possible the agency could save more buying the property and demolishing it than routing a $20 billion-plus project around it, which would force the future Westlake Station to one of the agency's deepest ever at around 135 feet.

While on the surface Krieg's memo appeared dismissive of the idea to switching to shorter automated stations, Kubly and Reed said the agency conceded some of their key points, and framed project risk all wrong, overlooking the shortcomings of its current approach.

Kubly and Reed said they didn't consider elevated rail in their white paper because they determined it would be too large of a change to reuse the existing environmental impact statement (EIS) documentation without significant additional work. They hoped ALR would largely repurpose the existing draft EIS since it was still in a tunnel with the same tunnel locations.
The draft EIS for Ballard Link was supposed to be released this year, but has been repeatedly delayed , with foot dragging from the Trump administration likely contributing.

The delays could be an opportunity to rethink approaches, but there's no sign that's the route the agency is going. Elevated rail could offer cost savings in West Seattle, or at least expose that the agency is not reasonably estimating the cost differential between tunneling and elevating lines.

West Seattle's Junction originally was envisioned as an elevated station, but Sound Transit converted it to an underground station under the excuse that it might actually be cheaper, while reducing neighborhood opposition related to aesthetic concerns and construction detours. Shortly thereafter, the agency revealed its preferred route has ballooned in cost by $1.6 billion . Cost reductions identified in March involved dropping the Avalan Station entirely.

"There's no universe that elevating should cost more than tunneling in West Seattle based on the current land use and extensive [City-owned right-of way or ROW]. Refusing to take any of the Fauntleroy ROW is an assumption that would be contested in any objective process," Kubly and Reed told The Urbanist . "But it was a red line for the electeds/local stakeholders actually negotiating. An elevated option in downtown could be a part of the solution. We think the better approach is not to prejudge an approach, but put them in competition, through the RFI.

Across the board, the agency is largely doubling down on existing approaches to keep ST3 projects moving, even as financial headwinds grow. That approach may end up working on some lines, but advocates are worried it's failing Ballard.

The board has prioritized building out the light rail spine to Tacoma and Everett – a corridor stretching more than 60 miles. Relatedly, those project face smaller delays. Sound Transit is expecting to open Tacoma Dome Link in 2035 – three years later than first planned. The agency is hoping to launch the first leg of the Everett Link extension (as far as Paine Field) in 2037. That's only one year later than promised during the ST3 campaign. The section from Paine Field to Everett Station would wait until 2041 under the phased opening plan.
Or as Kubly opined: "Don’t be surprised to read that the results from their RFI validate their current approach."
Correction : This article was updated at 1:12pm to note that the RFI deadline has been extended by one week to October 12.

articles.title: Paid Parking Could Expand to West Seattle, Upper Queen Anne
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) has unveiled proposals that would represent the largest expansion of paid on-street parking in the city at least a decade, impacting the Alaska Junction and Upper Queen Anne business districts. The changes are intended to make it easier to access curbside parking by increasing turnover, but the idea of starting to charge for something that was previously given away for free is already proving contentious among some neighbors and business leaders.
The rollout is being paired with an expansion of dedicated vehicle loading areas, ADA accessible parking, and intersection daylighting.

SDOT's paid parking program is structured around its goal of ensuring that customers in business districts are typically able to find one or two open parking spaces on any given block. The agency calibrates parking rates with the aim of hitting its availability target range: 70% to 85% occupancy.

Twice-annual adjustments in hourly rates up or down to meet that target have been a part of life in Seattle since 2010, as part of the performance-based parking program . Those adjustment generally do not get much attention, but adding paid parking where it doesn't exist is another matter.

After conducting a field study this past April, SDOT found that 26 out of 40 blocks in West Seattle's Alaska Junction were more than 85% full, with 11 blocks out of 22 in Upper Queen Anne also clearing the bar. Several blocks in both neighborhoods were also exceeding 100% occupancy, indicating high demand was leading drivers to park in non-designated areas in ways that could impact pedestrian safety.

SDOT's proposal is to implement hourly rates from $1 to $4 per hour across approximately a dozen blocks in Alaska Junction and eight blocks in Queen Anne, along with an expansion in time-limited free parking later into the evening until 8pm. Additional time-limited load zones are also set to be put in place in both neighborhoods.

Business owners are already pushing back on SDOT's proposal, at least when it comes to Upper Queen Anne. A September 23 letter signed by an array of business leaders and residents along Queen Anne Avenue asked the department to keep on-street parking free, citing potential negative impacts that could come from adding an "additional barrier" to business access. Signees to the letter included the owners of Queen Anne Book Company, Betty Restaurant, Aluel Cellars, Bounty Kitchen, Stuhlberg's giftshop, and the director of the Queen Anne Farmer's Market.

"The businesses and organizations signing this letter are united in asking the City not to introduce paid parking on Queen Anne Avenue," the letter stated. "Free and accessible street parking is an attractive feature of the Queen Anne business district for visitors, customers, and neighborhood residents. It makes it easier to stop for a meal, run an errand, visit a local shop, attend an appointment, or spend time in the neighborhood. We are concerned that introducing paid parking would diminish that advantage and create an additional barrier to visiting local businesses."

The same letter pushed back on the idea that high occupancy rates at parking stalls in front of Queen Anne businesses do not translate to automatic support for the idea of managing that demand through pricing.

"We also want to be clear that high parking demand along Queen Anne Avenue should not be interpreted as support from the business community for paid parking," it continued. "We support improving parking availability and turnover, but paid parking is not the only tool available. Better enforcement of existing time limits, appropriately located loading zones, short- term pickup spaces, accessible parking, and adjustments to existing parking restrictions should be fully utilized before paid parking is considered."

While a paid parking program is intended to increase access to the curb allowing visitors coming by car to more easily patronize local businesses, data shows that the majority of visitors to either business district are not arriving by car at all. SDOT surveys from earlier this year found that 66% of respondents in Alaska Junction and 61% in Queen Anne arrived by walking, biking, or taking transit. This suggests that business owners could be overrepresenting the number of customers who would be deterred by having parking meters on a street.

Outside of Seattle's downtown neighborhoods, paid parking programs are relatively rare, with only a few other business districts currently requiring drivers to pay to use public curbspace. Currently just 2% of Seattle streets have parking meters at all, one main reason that a neighborhood-by-neighborhood expansion of the program is likely to be controversial, with business owners used to the way things have been operating for decades.

When it comes to Alaska Junction, paid parking has been a topic that comes up about once a decade, becoming a lightning rod every time. In both 2009 and 2018, SDOT declined to implement parking meters in the neighborhood, citing stall occupancy rates that didn't yet meet the 80% threshold. But parking demand is increasing in the neighborhood, with average parking occupancy in the 5pm hour creeping up from 75% in 2017 to 91% this year.
SDOT is accepting feedback on the parking proposals for both neighborhoods, with any changes set to be implemented in 2027.

articles.title: Health giant’s new addition to 15th Ave streetscape? Fake flowers
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Thanks to neighbor Tammy Jo for the picture
Hopefully these new Capitol Hill flowers are not permanent-e .

Neighbors in the CHS Facebook Group have made note of a chintzy new addition to Kaiser Permanente’s Capitol Hill campus just as the health giant is about to embark on $2.5 million in clinical upgrades to its 15th Ave facilities.
“Kaiser on 15th has filled their planters with plastic flowers,” Tim notes . “Not at all tacky.”
Others agreed this may be a case where phony flowers are not better than nothing.

Whether any hospital officials are appreciating the sarcasm is not known. CHS is trying to sort out who at the California-based integrated managed care consortium to contact about the new landscaping.

The strange cost-saving measure comes as Kaiser is preparing major renovations within the main 15th and Thomas hospital complex including a $2.12 million Level 1 overhaul and supply conversions following its announcement that it would hold off on ER billing changes and add 25 inpatient beds, increasing capacity from 18 to 43 across intensive care, telemetry, and medical–surgical units.

Kaiser Permanente’s relationship with the surrounding neighborhood could also use some care. The health provider has been touting efforts to fill its street-fronting spaces with new businesses but the spaces have remained empty over recent years. Meanwhile, its complex surface parking lots remain underutilized neighborhood spaces .
A more than $400 million planned campus overhaul still on the books following Kaiser’s 2017 acquisition of Group Health has also, apparently, been downsized.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, October 5–11
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Nathalie Graham, Amanda Manitach, and Dave Segal
paras: (COMMUNITY) The annual Week Without Driving kicked off on October 1 and runs through October 8. Are you participating? Even if you haven’t yet, it’s not too late. It’s a fun challenge: Can you get around your city without a car? You’ll have to rely on the bus, a bike, or your own two feet. How long can you go? It’s a good way to appreciate the services at our fingertips, especially with Seattle Prop. 1 on the ballot next month. That proposition will raise sale tax to renew and expand the Seattle Transit Measure that funds our bus service. You better vote yes. Week Without Driving will show you why. If you’re looking for a specific Week Without Driving event, check out the Nondrivers Alliance’s event with law professor Michael Pollack , the author of Sidewalk Nation: The Life and Law of America’s Most Overlooked Resource , on October 5 at the Husky Union Building on University of Washington’s campus. ( Husky Union Building, 6:30–8 pm, free with RSVP ) NATHALIE GRAHAM

(VISUAL ART) It’s fitting that Surge, an exhibition that pairs visual artists with scientists to make work about climate change, takes place at the Museum of Northwest Art, located in La Conner, Washington. Climate change isn’t just a hypothetical in the Skagit basin, a 3,115-square-mile watershed that extends from the Cascades to the Skagit Bay. It’s experienced firsthand as the sea spills over levees, roads go underwater, and the familiar ways of doing things are swept away. This is the fourth iteration of Surge, curated by Chloé Dye Sherpe, and it’s always fascinating to see what happens when artists spend quality time in the trenches with the climatologists, hydrologists, biologists, and governmental policymakers tracking the changes that directly affect our region. This year’s robust roster includes artists working across media, from neon and glass to painting and assemblage: Holly Ballard Martz, Kelsey Fernkopf and Steve Gilbert, Melinda Hurst Frye, Morgan Madison, Steve Jensen, Sue Danielson, and Niki Keenan, to name but a few. ( Museum of Northwest Art ) AMANDA MANITACH

(FILM) John Wilson is a documentarian of the absurd. On his endlessly fascinating HBO comedy docuseries How To with John Wilson , he delves deep into themes as far-reaching as the Mandela effect, scaffolding, and circumcision, pasting together disparate clips of footage into a kind of collage to hilarious effect as he narrates via voiceover. His investigations end up leading him to the most unexpected places and put the dizzying spectrum of humanity on full display. That’s why I’m so excited for his new film, The History of Concrete , in which he attempts to apply a formula for writing and selling a hit Hallmark-style movie to a documentary about, yes, concrete. If anyone can make this topic riveting, it’s him, and I’m willing to bet you’ll never look at a sidewalk the same way again. ( SIFF Cinema Uptown & Tasveer Film Center, times vary ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) America’s most uncompromising hip-hop group, New Jersey’s Dälek, have been enlightening and blowing minds since 1998. A staunch advocate for POC’s rights, MC Dälek (aka Will Brooks) trenchantly rails against oppression and strife, from now to centuries back, with an authoritative bellow and a conspiratorial sneer while he and producer/instrumentalist Mike Manteca fuse industrial noise, drone, and funk into towers of sonic power. Their newest album, 2026’s Brilliance of a Falling Moon , takes a flamethrower to the fa$cist ruling class. This decade’s awful times have motivated Dälek to rise to even higher heights of lyrical causticity and sonic brutality. After 28 years of public service in the underground-hip-hop trenches, they’ve proved themselves to be the true heirs to Public Enemy’s crown. ( Funhouse, 8 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL

(BOOKS) Last year, Top Chef fan favorite and lesbian heartthrob Melissa King released her James Beard Award-winning debut cookbook Cook Like a King . You may recall that she and the show’s host Padma Lakshmi sent the collective sapphic universe into a gay panic with their flirty Instagram banter while simultaneously promoting their books, plus there was a sultry Gomez and Morticia couple costume that ignited dating rumors. (They’re just friends, or so they claim…) Now, King is back with her memoir The Girl Who Became King . The book shares her story of growing up queer in a Shanghainese and Cantonese family in Los Angeles’s Gabriel Valley, her initiation into the high-stakes world of Michelin-starred restaurants, and her Top Chef journey. She’ll share her story with food writer, photographer, designer, and Little Fat Boy blogger Frankie Gaw at this event, hosted by Charlie’s Queer Books at Ballard Homestead. ( Ballard Homestead, 7 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(PARTY) Everyone knows that Halloween is gay Christmas, and this party at Asylum Collective for “lesbians, bisexuals, femmes, butches, trans girls, nonbinary babes, sapphics, spooky little freaks + the people who love themmmmm” is the perfect opportunity to celebrate. You can look forward to DJs, dancing, free candy, tarot reading, and tattoos. Costumes are strongly encouraged and there will be contests for the best dressed—channel your inner Carmilla by dressing up as a hot lesbian vampiress and dance your ass off to “Red Wine Supernova.” ( Asylum Collective, 9 pm–1 am, 21+ ) JULIANNE BELL
The Blair Witch Project: Film Screening and Q&A

(FILM) Even if you’re not a horror fan, you undoubtedly know The Blair Witch Project , thanks to its prescient marketing hoax campaign, which leveraged the early internet to blur the boundaries of fact and fiction. The 1999 low-budget sleeper hit, which was primarily shot over the course of eight days, takes the form of a found-footage pseudo-documentary and famously listed its actors as “deceased” or “missing.” It’s not just a stunt, though: The film is genuinely haunting and understands that the unseen is more terrifying than the most gruesome monster special effects could ever conjure. This special screening at the 5th Avenue Theatre is an opportunity to see it in all its unsettling glory on the big screen, followed by a Q&A session with original cast members Heather Donahue, Joshua Leonard, and Michael C. Williams (all three alive and well). ( 5th Avenue Theatre, 7:30 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

articles.title: Slog AM: Katie Wilson Is Impatient With Herself, Brazil Presidential Election Heads to Runoff, Orcs Protest Palantir
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: I am a global citizen. Just read my wedding diary . Maybe that’s why the news out of Brazil (where I started my career ) and Morocco (where much of my family is from) caught my eye this morning. Don’t worry, I’m also keeping an eye on Seattle City Hall’s budget haggling.

Katie Wilson “is as impatient as everyone else” about her slow pace of reform, including dismantling homeless encampments and enacting progressive taxation. Wilson sat down with Seattle Nice and acknowledged how she’s continuing the practice of dismantling homeless encampments without offering shelter to people evicted (aka, sweeps); the punitive pushing around of her predecessors. She stressed the importance of creating good “vibes” for the business community, and made some nuanced arguments about the role of the Seattle Police Department and Law Enforcement Assisted Diversion in arresting and referring our way out of the public drug market crisis ( worth a listen! ).

Sheriffs across WA shall remain unaccountable to Olympia: On Friday, Thurston County Superior Court Judge Christine Schaller blocked key elements of a law passed by the Legislature this year that set standards for sheriffs, a role that is usually elected, that required them to have five years of law enforcement experience and no serious convictions, to be at least 25 years old, and to undergo background checks. It also allowed for their removal from office. Schaller’s ruling is the latest blow to accountability for sheriffs from the courts.

Alleged Chinese spy arrested, faces charges related to surveilling Taiwanese official’s family in Seattle: KING5 reports that the woman allegedly rented a car in Seattle, drove to the person’s house, and photographed the family and their vehicle, according to US officials. The images were sent to a Chinese official on WeChat.

The first union on Capitol Hill: California Rep . Ro Khanna’s staff have unionized, Politico reports . It’s the first time workers in the US legislature have done so. And it only took four years after a union vote in the Democrat’s office to actually get it done.

Brazil’s elections keep rhyming with America’s. Every four years, the world watches in horror as Americans go to the polls in embarrassingly low numbers to determine how the US will meddle with or support their futures. We experience a tiny fragment of this. In Brazil, elections predict how much of the Amazon Rainforest will get cut down. I was glued to the Rio Times coverage of Brazil’s runoff election results for the past 24 hours. Incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has reduced deforestation significantly, CarbonBrief calculates. His former rival, Trump fan Jair Bolsonaro, led a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, got convicted, and is currently in jail . The election was between Lula and Bolsonaro’s son.

Bolsonaro’s son got more votes: Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, has been running in his father’s place to carry the torch in a political alliance that is pro-gun, pro-Bible, all-in on agriculture (including slash and burn operations in the Amazon). Flávio Bolsonaro won 47 percent of the recent election vs. Lula’s 45 percent. Since neither won a majority, there will be a runoff. Lula is a center-left leader way past his prime (he’s 80) who helped bring a generation of Brazilians out of poverty. He’s too damn old to inspire the left and, like Biden, didn’t trust anyone to pass the torch to on his admittedly shallow bench. Brazilian voters go back to the polls on Oct. 25 to decide between Bolsonaro Jr. and Lula.

Death-from-the-sky maker Shield AI is expanding in Seattle , GeekWire reports .One priority of Mayor Katie Wilson’s is to diversify the economy amid a potential slide in tech. Well, there’s always the defense industrial complex. Shield AI makes the X-BAT, an “AI-piloted strike fighter” that outranges a Lockheed Martin F-35A and drops 2,000-pound bombs ( like the ones used on Gaza ). It’s planning to expand production to a warehouse near SeaTac.

Meanwhile, out of work “orcs” tried to get work at Palantir’s Seattle office. The LOTR-inspired company is involved in ICE’s surveillance of protesters , and gets a lot of Army contracts . It’s the latest milquetoast protest from Climate Defiance:

Morocco’s first female Prime Minister enjoyed her first weekend in power, blessed by the patriarchy. The New York Times notes that King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the third female head of state in a North African country. At the same time, the NYT suggests Moroccan women generally aren’t advancing as quickly in society as their representatives. We’ll see if Moroccan feminism and empowerment can filter down.

Morocco is America’s oldest ally, in a way: It was the first to recognize US independence in 1777 . Back then, we asked (paid) them to let up on the piracy and they agreed. Lately, our deals have been about expanding colonialism. Morocco has agreed to recognize the State of Israel , in exchange for the US recognizing Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara, whose people are only tied to Morocco because of Spanish colonization and dictatorship. You may have seen some of the region if you watched The Odyssey .

Seattle-area ferries delayed or cancelled due to lack of crew: KOMO reports that many routes are down to one boat or out of service entirely. Check the latest WSDOT delays ; this morning there were a lot of cancelled Bremerton/Seattle boats.

articles.title: Nathan Vass’ Deciding to See: Washington State Book Awards Finalist
articles.author: Nathan Vass
paras: We urban planning and transit enthusiasts tend not to think of the street in terms of narrative. Most of the literature we digest on these favorite subjects of ours – the opening of a new train line, the behind-the-scenes of a housing development, the political importance of this or that measure and its effects – is in the form of articles or video essays, which have the luxury of being instantly producible, with up-to-the-minute observations and (ideally) journalism’s commitment to a minimum of editorializing. We think of journalism as the primary method of which to conceive of the street.

A 300-page book which took five years to write might seem an odd fit for the above landscape, especially a book that can’t be called journalism, even if it is nonfiction. But I think humans ultimately conceive of everything in terms of narrative.

We think of our days and our projects and our entire lives as stories, with arcs, in which we (of course) are the protagonist. We wish for happy endings, or at least edifying ones, and if we don’t get them we tell ourselves the story isn’t over yet. We are linear, time-based creatures, and in the same way we search for a story when watching one of the time-based art forms, even when there may not be one there at all (like dance), we frame how we think about our lives using the rules of narrative.

I think stories are the most powerful way to communicate. Paul Currington says opinions divide people; stories bring them together. In our (dis)information age, facts, or assertions masquerading as facts, have shown themselves to have limited value in changing minds.

If your family member is prejudiced, they won’t come around to your perspective when you dump data in their lap explaining how racism or sexism are shortsighted. They’ll come around because of primary experience happening in the one story they do care about, their own , the story of their life, as they get to know their coworker who’s from somewhere far away, or their friend’s child, who lives by different rules. The human element.

I didn’t write either of my books to change people’s minds. I wrote them to share a world I find interesting and underrepresented in the world of literature. I wrote them because there was so much life happening in this “lowbrow” space of unglamorous liminal life, so dense with incident and color and laughter and sorrow, and so few artists were transposing it to the “highbrow” space of probing literary reflection, of the word as art form.

I know there are others like me, but maybe too many of our great authors stay inside their offices, and too many of our best bus drivers don’t study comparative literature. Can I help it if I have interests and passions which have nothing to do with each other??

We know the power of stories, and we know the joy of sharing bus stories, which we humans will never stop telling each other, not as long as there’s transit in our lives. I’m frankly floored by the success my latest book continues to have – continuously bestselling in our city for over a year now, taught as a textbook at Seattle U, and now a Finalist for the 2026 Washington State Book Awards , alongside Rebecca Brown (Eep eep! I can die happy now) and others… all of this is thanks to you readers and enthusiasts, especially transit enthusiasts.

The Urbanist 's readers are my ideal audience: those of us interested in living as an urban collective, curious to see how the world of the street looks when viewed through the lens of art and narrative, searching for how we can live in the same forward direction, part of the same common project.
More press and interviews about the book here . Buy the book anywhere books are sold, including our own Elliott Bay Books, where I recently signed all copies :)

articles.title: Op-Ed: Fill in the Spring Boulevard Gap with a Trail
articles.author: Eastside Urbanism
paras: Do arterial roads belong in city parks? That is one of the key questions the Bellevue City Council will need to consider during its October 6 budget deliberations on transportation projects. The staff has presented an option to give full funding (for the first time) of $74.8 million to the one-third-mile, two-lane Spring Boulevard “gap” with a new 0.1% sales tax . But this "Zone 3" plan is colliding with another emerging project on the same land: the BelRed Neighborhood Park .

We believe roads like that do not belong in a park. The City should instead plan a pedestrian/bicycle-only trail. But before we make that case, let’s step back to understand the historical precedents and the reasons the City wants to build the road.

Bellevue, the self-described “City in a Park,” has many beautiful parks, such as Bannerwood, Crossroads, Downtown, Highland, Lake Hills, Lakemont, Mercer Slough, Meydenbauer, Robinswood, Surrey Downs, Weowna, and Wilburton Hill. The fact that none of these parks have arterial roads going through them shows Bellevue residents have been prioritizing parks over cars for as long as the city has existed.

Wilburton Hill Park presents a particularly enticing cut-through opportunity to extend 124th Ave south of Main St to the Lake Hills Connector. The City considered this project many years ago, but it was so forcefully rejected by residents that the policy to not do it is now cemented as S-WI-15 in the Wilburton subarea plan .

Downtown Park is another interesting case to examine. Before building that park in the mid 1980s, the City removed a large section of 102nd Avenue, which had bisected the site for decades. As a video from the time makes clear, the City wanted to create a big, green meadow that would last forever, and it would have been unthinkable to compromise that vision for a few seconds of driver convenience.

Downtown Bellevue of the 1980’s, like BelRed today , was a mostly commercial district just beginning its journey to the mixed-use, high-rise urban center it is now. The successful Downtown Park strategy of prioritizing urban green space provides a model worthy of replication in BelRed.

So if Bellevue has never allowed arterials in parks in the past, then why is it planning to do so now? The City laid out the purpose of Spring Boulevard's Zone 3 in an application for a federal grant in 2024. According to the City, the project would:

We dispute the 2-3 minute reduction for drivers. Google Maps estimates the total driving time for the existing route along BelRed Road at just two minutes , so the reduction in driving time would be even less. Also, cars on the new route would often need to yield at crosswalks in the busy park, further eroding any small improvement in driving times.

Apart from that exaggerated driving time reduction, all of the other justifications for the project would also apply to a trail. In fact, if the City wants to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a trail would be better than a road because it would be more effective at encouraging travel by bicycle without creating the infamous induced traffic demand associated with new roads. And if the City wants to attract investment, a park without an arterial would be more appealing to residents, and therefore more attractive for housing developers and employers.

The Spring Boulevard plan was initially presented to the City Council in 2011. At that time, there were plans for another large park in BelRed . It was tentatively called Northup Meadows, and it would have been on the site of what instead became Sound Transit’s train base . Since the plan for that park fell apart, the other BelRed park (in Spring Boulevard’s path) has gained a new degree of importance as the only park in the rapidly-growing area. It is only appropriate to re-evaluate the need for Spring Boulevard (Zone 3) in light of the significantly changed conditions.
To put our case simply: BelRed Park is a wonderful idea and letting drivers cut through would wreck it.

Parents visiting the park would need to constantly worry about safety as distracted drivers speed by. Their kids couldn’t roam freely and play. Picnicking families would have to put up with constant road noise and backfiring car exhausts. Green grass would cede to hot asphalt. Even with a crosswalk or two, people would try to cross the road everywhere, a recipe for pedestrian injuries. Being close to light rail stations could make BelRed Park one of the best outdoor event spaces in the city, but nobody wants a bunch of loud cars cutting through their event.

Now let’s talk about money. Spring Boulevard's Zone 3 project would cost about $75 million . Last year, Bellevue staff estimated a trail cost at $18-20 million ( on page 12 of these minutes ). In other words, about 75% of the project budget would be directed exclusively at the goal of trying to save drivers a few seconds of travel time.

With a trail, all of the City’s other goals could be achieved at 25% the cost. (Since most of that cost is for land acquisition, and the land owner is Sound Transit , who has been supportive of parks and pedestrian infrastructure around their stations, we might be able to save even more money by making a deal with Sound Transit to put a trail on their land without buying it.)

Think about your favorite park. Now imagine what it would be like with an arterial road going directly through it. That’s what the Spring Boulevard Zone 3 project would do to BelRed Park, before it even has a chance to show how great it can be.
